summary: Australian reviewers largely agree the Sealion 7 is one of the most convincing mainstream electric SUVs yet from a Chinese brand, praising its spacious, well-finished cabin, strong value against the Tesla Model Y, and a confident five-star ANCAP safety rating. The dual-motor Performance adds genuinely quick acceleration while keeping the comfortable, easy-to-live-with character of the range. Verdicts are more mixed on dynamics, with several outlets noting body roll, a ride that can feel soggy on the open road and jiggly around town, and lingering infotainment glitches.
pros: Spacious, well-finished cabin with generous rear-seat room and dual driver displays
Strong value against the Tesla Model Y, undercutting it while matching much of its specification
Five-star ANCAP safety rating (2025) with comprehensive standard driver-assist tech
Performance variant adds genuine pace (4.5s 0-100km/h) without losing everyday comfort
cons: Noticeable body roll and a ride that reviewers describe as soggy at speed and jiggly around town
Some tech gremlins and infotainment software glitches reported in early ownership
Real-world range and efficiency trail the claimed WLTP figures by a noticeable margin
BYD's Australian resale value and dealer/service network are still relatively unproven for the brand

summary: The Sealion 8 is BYD's first three-row model in Australia, a large seven-seat plug-in hybrid that undercuts the Kia Sorento PHEV and Mazda CX-80 PHEV by roughly $11,000-$14,000 at the entry point while claiming far more electric range on paper — up to 152km, though on the lenient NEDC cycle, as BYD publishes no WLTP figure. Reviewers broadly agree on the value case, the presentation of the cabin and the generous second row, and CarsGuide judges the 359kW AWD grades' performance more than a family SUV needs. Where they diverge is ride and refinement: CarExpert rates it quiet and well-resolved, while Chasing Cars flags inconsistent damping and cabin noise and CarsGuide finds the comfort-biased ride short on body control.
pros: The 35.6kWh battery in the AWD grades is the largest plug-in pack in any seven-seat SUV sold here, if only just ahead of the 34.5kWh Chery Tiggo 9 PHEV Ultimate and Jaecoo J8 SHS, and roughly two and a half times the Kia Sorento PHEV's 13.8kWh; BYD claims 152km (NEDC) of electric running from it.
Sharp entry pricing: $56,990 before on-roads for the Dynamic FWD against $70,880 for the cheapest Kia Sorento PHEV and $68,100 for the Mazda CX-80 PHEV Touring.
Braked towing of 1800kg (Dynamic FWD) or 2000kg (both AWD grades) comfortably beats the Kia Sorento PHEV's 1010kg, which is the usual weak point of a plug-in seven-seater.
Warranty is six years/150,000km, and the high-voltage battery carries a separate eight-year/160,000km cover.

Combined tailpipe CO2 of 22-24g/km puts every grade far under Victoria's 120g/km green-passenger-car duty threshold, the 1.0-1.1L/100km label passes the LCT fuel-efficient test, and all three list prices sit below the $80,809 ordinary LCT threshold so no luxury car tax is payable.
cons: Only 270 litres of boot behind the third row — enough for a school run, not a seven-up holiday — and there is no spare wheel at all, just a puncture repair kit.

Every electric range figure is NEDC. BYD publishes no WLTP number in Australia, New Zealand or Singapore and the car is not yet sold in the UK; RACV's own conversion puts the realistic equivalents nearer 88km (FWD) and 130km (AWD).

The plug-in compromise is visible in BYD's own numbers: the 1.0-1.1L/100km label assumes a charged battery, and BYD quotes 5.3L/100km (FWD) or 6.3L/100km (AWD) once the pack falls below 25 per cent — so a buyer who cannot charge at home is simply running a 2.3-2.6 tonne SUV on petrol.

The third row is described by CarsGuide as strictly for smaller kids, with tight access, and Chasing Cars criticises cabin noise, front-seat support and the reliance on touchscreen controls for basic functions.
CarsGuide calls the 359kW AWD grades' performance irrelevant in a family car, yet they carry a $7,000-$14,000 premium over the Dynamic FWD and add around 265kg of kerb weight.

summary: Australian reviewers treat the Shark 6 as the ute that reset the segment's value equation: it was the first plug-in hybrid dual-cab sold here, and at $57,900-$62,900 before on-roads for the Premium and Performance pickups it undercuts the Ford Ranger PHEV's upper grades while out-accelerating any diesel rival. The consistent caveat is capability rather than comfort - payload sits below the class norm, the 1.5-litre Premium stops at 2500kg braked towing, and there is no low-range transfer case, so reviewers steer heavy haulers and serious off-roaders elsewhere; reviewers split on the ride, which some call SUV-like and Chasing Cars found lumpy over bigger bumps. BYD has also run repeated drive-away campaigns on the Shark 6 (currently $4,000 off to 21 December 2026), which makes list-price resale harder to read than for the segment's established diesels.
pros: Strong value for a plug-in dual-cab: the Premium pickup is $57,900 before on-roads, about $3,000 under the Ranger PHEV Sport while making far more power (321kW/650Nm, or 350kW/700Nm in the $62,900 Performance)

Electric range holds up in the real world: Chasing Cars covered about 80km on battery alone against an 89km WLTP rating for the 1.5-litre, enough to cover a typical Melbourne commute without the engine starting
8-year/160,000km battery warranty runs two years past the 6-year/150,000km unconditional vehicle warranty, on long 12-month/20,000km service intervals
Five-star ANCAP and coil-sprung double wishbones front and rear, which make it quieter and more composed on smooth roads than any leaf-sprung diesel dual-cab
The Performance delivers the segment-benchmark 3500kg braked towing for $5,000 over the Premium, and CarExpert found it stayed stable with a 2.8-tonne caravan behind it
cons: Payload trails the class: 790kg on the Premium and as little as 725kg on the Performance, against more than 900kg for most dual-cab rivals

With the battery depleted it uses 9.6L/100km (1.5-litre, WLTP) or 10.5L/100km (Performance), not the 1.3-2.0L/100km label figure - a buyer who cannot charge at home pays diesel-ute running costs for premium 95RON petrol
No low-range transfer case and limited articulation; reviewers found it out of its depth on the hardest tracks even with the Performance's new Crawl mode, which only partly mimics low range
BYD Australia quotes 100km electric range for the 1.5-litre on the old NEDC cycle; the same truck rates 89km on WLTP in the UK, and the Performance 80km
2.7-2.8 tonne kerb weight and a ladder-frame PHEV driveline push Melbourne comprehensive quotes above comparable mid-size PHEV SUVs, with quotes on the Premium reported past $2,000

summary: Cadillac's first Australian model is a 2.8-tonne dual-motor electric SUV that a permanent $32,000 cut has re-priced from $122,000 to $90,000 before on-road costs, dropping it under the fuel-efficient LCT threshold and into FBT-exempt novated-lease territory. Reviewers agree on the hushed ride, the 530km WLTP range and the distinctive styling, but split hard on the cabin: CarExpert and carsales rate it genuinely luxurious, while Chasing Cars judges the materials and rear-seat packaging not good enough at any price. The unresolved risks are a three-outlet retail network across Australia and New Zealand, no tow rating at all, and the resale damage the cut inflicts on every car sold before it.
pros: The permanent cut from $122,000 to $90,000 before on-road costs puts it under the $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT threshold, so it now qualifies for the FBT exemption on a novated lease — it did not at launch.
530km WLTP from a 102kWh pack, and a 22.1kW three-phase AC onboard charger roughly double the 11kW most rivals fit, so a full charge on three-phase takes about five hours rather than overnight-plus.
793 litres behind the second row and 1,722 litres folded, against 526/1,536L in a Polestar 4 and 333L behind row two in a seven-seat Kia EV9.

Five years unlimited-kilometre warranty plus five years of complimentary scheduled servicing at 12-month/12,000km intervals, an eight-year/160,000km battery warranty, and a year of free public charging upgradable to three years or a 7kW home charger.

Genuinely quiet: active noise cancellation that pre-empts road impacts and a 19-speaker AKG Studio system with Dolby Atmos are what every Australian reviewer singles out, alongside 388kW/610Nm and 0-100km/h in 5.3 seconds.
cons: The $32,000 cut is a resale problem as much as a bargain — every Lyriq sold at $117,000 to $124,000 was re-based overnight to $90,000, and Cadillac does not report sales to VFACTS, so there is no local residual data to argue with.
Not rated to tow anything in Australia, where a Kia EV9 pulls 2,500kg braked and a Zeekr 7X 2,000kg.

Three retail outlets across Australia and New Zealand — the Rosebery Experience Centre in Sydney, a Port Melbourne test-drive venue and Auckland — with the promised Brisbane site still unopened, so servicing and panel repair mean a long trip for most buyers.
Super Cruise is not approved for Australian roads and the adaptive cruise ships without lane centring; there is also no head-up display and no native navigation at $90,000.

At 2,774kg and a claimed 22.5kWh/100km it is markedly thirstier than a Polestar 4 Dual Motor's 18.7kWh/100km, and Chasing Cars rates the rear seat's high floor and hard ISOFIX bracing covers as genuinely uncomfortable.

summary: The Optiq is the cheapest way into General Motors' relaunched Cadillac brand in Australia, and reviewers consistently praise its distinctive, well-finished cabin, quiet running and unusually generous standard equipment for $80,000 before on-road costs. The consensus criticism is just as consistent: 425km of WLTP range and a 110kW DC charging ceiling are the weakest numbers among luxury mid-size electric SUVs on sale here, and Australia takes the superseded 224kW powertrain rather than the US car's 328kW update. Opinion divides mainly on the ride, which most describe as composed and connected but firmer and less plush than the badge implies.
pros: At $80,000 before on-road costs it undercuts the BMW iX3 ($89,900), Genesis GV60 ($88,300) and Lexus RZ ($84,500), and sits well under the $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT threshold that governs the novated-lease FBT exemption
Genuinely big for the class: a 744-litre boot with the rear seats up (1603 litres folded) and a 2954mm wheelbase that reviewers rate for near-limousine rear knee room

Heavily specified in its single grade — 33-inch curved display with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto (features GM deleted from its US EVs), 19-speaker AKG Dolby Atmos audio, heated/ventilated/massaging front seats, Brembo front brakes, panoramic glass roof and 21-inch wheels
22.1kW three-phase AC charging is unusually quick for the segment and adds roughly 100km of range per hour at home, which softens the weak DC rate for overnight chargers
Five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty with no servicing strings attached, an eight-year/160,000km battery warranty, and a five-star Euro NCAP result (2025) scoring 83% for adult occupant protection
cons: 110kW is the lowest DC fast-charging peak of any luxury mid-size electric SUV sold in Australia — a Polestar 4 accepts 200kW — so road trips mean noticeably longer stops
425km of WLTP range is short for an $80,000 EV in 2026, and the 19.9kWh/100km WLTP consumption claim is high for the class (CarExpert measured 17.9kWh/100km on test)

Australia gets the superseded 224kW/480Nm dual-motor drivetrain while the US MY26 car has 328kW/675Nm and 150kW charging, and GM Australia has given no timing for bringing the update here; the Optiq-V is ruled out entirely

Firm-riding on 21-inch wheels with no adaptive dampers available, which several Australian reviewers judged short of the plushness a luxury badge implies, and the steering is described as vague on-centre

New-brand ownership risk: Cadillac does not report Australian sales, retails through a handful of metropolitan experience centres, permanently cut the larger Lyriq's price by $32,000 during 2026, and had still not confirmed Optiq service pricing at launch

summary: The Vistiq is Cadillac's three-row flagship EV for Australia, sold in a single fully-loaded Platinum grade at $116,000 before on-road costs — sharp enough to undercut a Kia EV9 GT-Line and well under a Volvo EX90 or Hyundai Ioniq 9. Australian reviewers rate the cabin, the AKG audio and the genuinely usable third row highly, and are near-unanimous that the drivetrain is far quicker than the class needs. Where they diverge is whether the Australia-only 91kWh pack is enough: 461km of WLTP range and a 130kW DC charging ceiling are both below what the price and the badge imply, and the brand's tiny local footprint makes resale the open question.
pros: At $116,000 before on-roads it undercuts the Kia EV9 GT-Line ($121,000), Hyundai Ioniq 9 and Volvo EX90 while arriving in top Platinum trim only — 22-inch wheels, adaptive air suspension, rear-wheel steering, four-zone climate, a 33-inch curved display and 23-speaker AKG audio are all standard, with no options ladder to climb
Third row is adult-sized rather than the usual '5+2' afterthought, and the second-row captain's chairs leave a walk-through aisle to reach it
459kW/880Nm dual-motor AWD covers 0-100km/h in 4.2 seconds, quicker than any EV9 including the GT
Five years of complimentary scheduled servicing and roadside assistance comes on top of the 5-year/unlimited-km warranty, with the battery covered for 8 years/160,000km
cons: DC charging peaks at just 130kW — the US car gets 190kW, and the 800V Kia EV9 recharges materially faster, so long trips cost more time than the price suggests
461km WLTP from the Australia-only 91kWh usable pack (the US car gets 102kWh) trails the Kia EV9 Earth's 521km and the Ioniq 9, in a 5.2m SUV that is thirsty at a claimed 22kWh/100km
Six seats only in Australia — the US seven-seat bench is not offered — with 430L behind the third row and no front boot under the long bonnet
Resale is the brand risk: Cadillac sells through a handful of Australian stores and the closely related Lyriq took a permanent $32,000 price cut in 2026, which drags residuals across the range

summary: The Chery E5 (rebranded from Omoda E5 during 2025, with the Omoda name now reserved for a separate model line) is one of the cheapest new electric SUVs on sale in Australia, a small front-wheel-drive EV pitched on price and standard equipment rather than dynamic polish. Australian reviewers consistently praise its value, long warranty and well-equipped cabin, but mark it down for unsettled ride quality, an over-cautious safety-assist calibration, and a boot that trails class rivals. The range is a single Ultimate grade ($35,990 before on-roads, advertised nationally from $37,990 drive-away but $39,604 drive-away for a Melbourne postcode) with a 58.9kWh LFP battery and 430km WLTP range; a facelifted MY27 'New E5' is listed as coming soon but is not yet priced or orderable.
pros: One of the cheapest new electric SUVs on sale in Australia at $35,990 before on-roads, undercutting the BYD Atto 3 ($39,990) and Geely EX5 ($41,990)
Long ownership package: 7-year unlimited-km vehicle warranty and 8-year unlimited-km battery warranty, plus 7-year capped-price servicing
Well-equipped single grade: dual 12.3-inch screens, heated front and rear seats, heated steering wheel, Sony audio, power tailgate, sunroof and a full-size spare
430km WLTP range from a 58.9kWh LFP battery, with a heat pump and 155kW motor (0-100km/h in 7.6 seconds)
cons: Softly sprung, with body lean in corners and sharp bumps such as expansion joints upsetting the ride; reviewers split on whether it is jittery or comfortable around town
Safety-assist calibration is poor: lane centring that cannot hold the lane and can steer toward other vehicles, and a driver monitor that chimes at normal glances
Small 300-litre boot (to the cargo cover, seats up) trails the Atto 3's 440 litres and the Jaecoo J5 EV's 384 litres
Slow DC charging for the class: 80kW peak, about 30 minutes for 30-80%, and only 6.6kW single-phase AC
A facelifted MY27 E5 is listed as coming soon, so a current car may depreciate faster once it arrives

summary: The Tiggo 7 Super Hybrid is the cheapest plug-in hybrid SUV in this list at $32,990 before on-road costs, and Australian reviewers agree the powertrain is the reason to buy it: an 18.4kWh LFP battery good for about 90km of WLTP electric range, 40kW DC fast charging almost nobody else offers at this price, and roughly 4-6L/100km once the battery is flat. Where they part company is the chassis and the software — NRMA, CarExpert and The Beep all criticise the stiff, jarring ride, the disconnected steering and an occasional driveline shunt, while carsales and CarsGuide are more forgiving on the basis of what it costs. Nobody argues it is good to drive; the case rests on running costs, the seven-year warranty and a price Chery has now cut by $5,000 since launch.
pros: About 90km of WLTP electric range from the 18.4kWh LFP pack — more than a BYD Sealion 5 Essential's 71km and enough for most Melbourne commutes on electricity alone
40kW DC fast charging (30-80 per cent in about 20 minutes) plus 3.3kW vehicle-to-load, where the BYD Sealion 6 and Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV have no DC capability at all

Stays efficient with the battery depleted: Chery UK's combined figure of 47.1mpg (6.0L/100km) is the charge-sustaining number, Chery Australia told CarExpert 6.0L/100km was realistic, and Australian testers recorded 3.8-6.0L/100km, so the car is not punishing for a buyer who forgets to plug in
Seven-year unlimited-kilometre warranty with no dealer-servicing condition, a separate eight-year unlimited-kilometre battery warranty, and capped-price servicing quoted at $3,174 across seven years

Five-star ANCAP rating applied to petrol and Super Hybrid Tiggo 7 variants built from June 2025, and at $32,990 and $36,990 before on-roads both grades sit far below the $75,000 FBT cap and the $80,809 ordinary LCT threshold
cons: Ride and steering are the consistent complaint: NRMA calls the suspension stiff and jarring with steering that gives almost no feedback, CarExpert reports unexplained driveline power surges like a clutch dump, and The Beep describes vague steering and lazy throttle response

The plug-in packaging costs you the underfloor storage and the spare wheel entirely — the Super Hybrid gets a tyre repair kit only, where the petrol Tiggo 7 has a two-level boot floor and underfloor bin
No braked tow rating published — Chery quotes only 750kg unbraked, so a caravan or a boat rules the car out where a petrol mid-size SUV would not

The 1.4L/100km label figure is a laboratory number that assumes you start every trip charged; without home charging you are running a 1,788kg SUV on its petrol engine at 4-6L/100km and the plug-in premium never pays back

Chery has cut the national drive-away price by $5,000 on both grades since launch (Urban $39,990 to $34,990) and still stacks a $2,000 cashback on top until 21 December 2026, so the street price keeps resetting and resale is unproven

summary: The Tiggo 8 Super Hybrid is the cheapest seven-seat plug-in hybrid on sale in Australia, and Australian reviewers agree the powertrain is the reason to buy it: a 1.5-litre turbo petrol engine and 150kW motor in a single-speed dedicated hybrid transmission, an 18.4kWh LFP battery good for 90km of WLTP electric range, and 5.6-6.1L/100km on test once the battery is flat. Where they split is the chassis and the third row — CarsGuide and EV Central rate the value and the powertrain calibration highly, while Chasing Cars, carsales and the NRMA mark down a floaty, underdamped ride, screen-buried controls and a rearmost row that has no top-tether or ISOFIX anchorages at all. As a two-row family SUV with occasional seats seven and eight it is compelling; as a genuine three-row people mover it is compromised by 117 litres of boot behind the third row and kerbside-only access to it.
pros: The cheapest seven-seat PHEV in Australia at $42,990 before on-road costs for the Urban — roughly $25,000 under a Mitsubishi Outlander Exceed PHEV and about $30,000 under a Kia Sorento PHEV, both of which also seat seven

90km of WLTP electric-only range (56 miles, Chery UK) from the 18.4kWh LFP pack, enough to cover most Melbourne commutes on electricity (Chasing Cars saw 68km in mixed real driving), and 40kW DC fast charging takes 30-80 per cent in about 20 minutes, which a BYD Sealion 6 at 18kW cannot match

Seven-year/unlimited-kilometre warranty with no dealer-servicing-exclusivity condition, plus a separate eight-year/unlimited-kilometre high-voltage battery warranty and seven years of capped-price servicing totalling $3,174.15

The petrol engine drives the wheels directly through the DHT in parallel mode rather than acting only as a generator, so consumption on a flat battery settles at 5.6-6.1L/100km on Australian tests instead of collapsing the way a range-extender's does

Five-star ANCAP rating from 2025 covering all variants including the Super Hybrid, with 86 per cent child occupant protection and nine airbags, and at $46,990 the top Ultimate still sits about $34,000 under the ordinary $80,809 LCT threshold
cons: Only 117 litres of boot with all seven seats in use — less than a Kia Sorento's 179 litres and a Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV's 191 litres — so the third row and the weekly shop are effectively mutually exclusive

No top-tether or ISOFIX anchorages in the third row at all, which ANCAP explicitly flags, and third-row access is via the kerbside door only, putting children out on the traffic side on a right-hand kerb

The 1.3L/100km combined label figure is meaningless in use: Chasing Cars recorded 5.6L/100km once the battery was flat and CarsGuide's long-term Ultimate logged 6.1 and then 6.9L/100km at the pump, so a buyer without home charging is running a 1.9-tonne seven-seater on premium 95-octane at ordinary-SUV cost

No braked towing rating whatsoever — 750kg unbraked only — where the 2.0-litre petrol Tiggo 8 and most seven-seat rivals are rated for a caravan or a boat, and neither grade carries a spare wheel (inflator kit only)

Reviewers split on the ride, which Chasing Cars found slow to settle over potholes where CarExpert found it plush, the climate and drive-mode functions are buried in the touchscreen, and Chery's national drive-away pricing plus a $3,000 cashback running to 21 December 2026 leaves resale value unproven

summary: The Tiggo 9 Super Hybrid is Chery Australia's flagship: a 4.8-metre seven-seat plug-in hybrid in a 225kW front-drive Elite at $52,990 and a 315kW all-wheel-drive Ultimate at $59,990 before on-road costs, though Chery advertises only postcode drive-away prices that also carry a dealer delivery charge. Reviewers agree the powertrain is the story — the Ultimate's 34.5kWh pack is rated at 140km WLTP (CarExpert measured 138km) and takes 71kW DC charging — while the Elite's 19kWh pack manages about 80km. Where they diverge is the body around it: CarExpert praises the value and equipment but marks down a cramped third row its curtain airbags did not cover, firm ride and vague steering, CarsGuide found the ride comfortable, and there is still no ANCAP rating.
pros: 140km of WLTP electric range on the Ultimate, from a 34.5kWh pack, against a Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV's 84km, with CarExpert recording 138km in hot weather before the engine started
71kW DC fast charging on the Ultimate (41kW on the Elite) plus 6.6kW AC, where the Outlander PHEV, Kia Sorento PHEV and BYD Sealion 6 offer no meaningful DC capability at all
Seven-year/unlimited-kilometre warranty with no dealer-servicing condition, a separate eight-year/unlimited-kilometre high-voltage battery warranty, and seven years of capped-price servicing
1500kg braked tow rating and a 70-litre tank on both grades, plus 315kW/580Nm in the Ultimate, where the Tiggo 7 and Tiggo 8 Super Hybrids are not rated to tow anything braked

At $59,990 the top Ultimate sits more than $20,000 below the ordinary $80,809 LCT threshold and undercuts a seven-seat Kia Sorento PHEV by roughly $25,000, so no luxury car tax is payable on either grade
cons: Only 143 litres of boot with all seven seats up, less than a Kia Sorento's 179 litres and a Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV's 191 litres, and CarExpert found the curtain airbags do not cover third-row occupants (Chery's own page now claims full-length curtains, but its spec sheet is unchanged); there is no ANCAP rating either way

The 1.4-1.5L/100km combined label is a fiction for anyone who cannot charge: CarExpert measured 6.3L/100km and CarsGuide 7.1L/100km once the battery was flat, and the car demands 95-octane premium, so a 2.2-tonne SUV with no home charger costs about as much to fuel as a petrol large SUV
The Elite's 19kWh pack is rated at 90km only on the lenient NEDC cycle; CarExpert estimates 75-80km in real driving, barely half the Ultimate's, for a $7,000 saving

CarExpert criticises a firm, unsettled ride over consecutive bumps, wooden and vague steering and cheap shiny plastics between the front seats, and rates the third row too tight and awkward to reach for regular seven-seat use; neither grade carries a spare wheel

Chery discounts hard, with $3,000 cashback on both grades in late 2026 and only drive-away prices advertised, so residual values are unproven and the depreciation assumption here is the Chery brand curve rather than observed

summary: The Formentor VZe is the sole plug-in hybrid in Cupra's coupe-styled small SUV range, and the MY26 update gave it a 19.7kWh usable battery (25.8kWh gross) for a claimed 114km of electric range — enough that most Melbourne commuters would rarely start the 1.5-litre engine. Reviewers agree the second-generation drivetrain is smooth and genuinely quick at 200kW, but they split on whether it is worth $68,990: CarExpert found it the least resolved car in the range to drive, with heavy steering and a soft-front/stiff-rear ride, and named the Skoda Kodiaq PHEV, a bit cheaper with similar electric range, as its biggest challenge. The recurring practical complaint is that the battery costs it a quarter of its boot and its spare wheel.
pros: 114km of claimed electric range from a 19.7kWh usable battery is roughly double the previous VZe's 58km and beats every PHEV SUV near the price — Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV claims 86km, Mazda CX-60 PHEV 76km
50kW DC fast charging plus 11kW AC is rare on a plug-in hybrid: most PHEV rivals, including the Outlander and CX-60, have no DC capability at all
200kW/400Nm and 7.2sec to 100km/h makes it quicker than the 150kW petrol Formentor V that sits $11,500 below it
Five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional — it is not tied to servicing inside the Cupra network — and the high-voltage battery is separately covered for 8 years/160,000km
Priced at $68,990 before on-road costs, it is rated at 1.7L/100km and 38g/km CO2, so it sits under the $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT threshold and qualifies for Victoria's flat green-car stamp duty rate
cons: The battery cuts the boot from roughly 450 litres in the petrol Formentor to 345 litres, and deletes the spare wheel entirely — CarsGuide lists 'small boot in PHEV' and 'no spare wheel' as its headline dislikes

Once the battery is flat it is an ordinary 1.5-litre turbo hauling over 1,750kg, and the 1.7L/100km label figure is meaningless — the European battery-empty WLTP figure is 5.6L/100km and Auto Motor und Sport measured 7.1L/100km in hybrid mode, so the economics collapse for a buyer without home charging

CarExpert judged the VZe the most disconnected car in the Formentor range to drive, citing heavy, feel-free steering from the extra front-axle mass and suspension that is too soft at the front and too stiff at the rear

The plug-in hybrid lost its FBT exemption on 1 April 2025, and Cupra's own MY24 run-out saw the previous VZe cut from $64,990 to $47,990 drive-away — with Formentor sales down 61.3 per cent in the first half of 2026, resale risk is real
No vehicle-to-load outlet, a 40-litre fuel tank that limits touring range once the battery is depleted, and a 1,700kg braked tow rating

summary: The Tavascan is Cupra's only battery-electric model in Australia, a coupe-roofed mid-size SUV on the same MEB platform as the Volkswagen ID.5 and Skoda Enyaq, now sold in three grades after the MY27 update added a 58kWh LFP entry V below the 77kWh Endurance and dual-motor VZ. Australian reviewers rate its steering and body control above most rivals and CarsGuide singles out the ride as a surprise strength, though Chasing Cars found the Endurance's firm rear suspension tiring and reviewers still criticise the 135kW DC charging peak, cabin squeaks and the lack of connected services. The update also raised the Endurance by $5,500 and lifted the VZ to $75,490, just over the $75,000 FBT cap that applies from April 2027.
pros: Sharp chassis: Chasing Cars found the Endurance 'excels' through corners with little body roll and accurate steering, and CarsGuide called the ride quality the car's biggest surprise, with the VZ's adaptive dampers giving a supple ride

The new V opens the range at $55,490 before on-road costs, about $3,400 under a Tesla Model Y RWD per Chasing Cars, with heated power front seats, Sennheiser audio, a 360-degree camera and 20-inch wheels standard
540 litres seats-up and 1,550 litres seats-down on every grade, with a low, flat boot floor and rear space CarsGuide rated ample for adults up to about 180cm
Five-year unlimited-kilometre factory warranty with no Cupra-network servicing condition stated, plus 8 years/160,000km on the high-voltage battery with a 70 per cent capacity floor

The VZ is rated to tow 1,800kg braked against 1,000kg for the V and Endurance, and adds 250kW all-wheel drive (0-100km/h in 5.5 seconds), DCC adaptive dampers, a fixed panoramic roof and matrix high beams
cons: The VZ at $75,490 sits $490 over the $75,000 FBT full-exemption cap that applies to novated leases from 1 April 2027, while the Endurance rose $5,500 to $66,490 in the MY27 update (the former $4,500 Interior Package is now standard)
Slow DC charging: 135kW peak on the 77kWh grades, which Chasing Cars called disappointing, and just 105kW on the V's 58kWh LFP pack

Chasing Cars measured 18.3kWh/100km on the Endurance, implying about 421km per charge, and CarExpert saw 19.8kWh/100km in the VZ against its 17.4kWh/100km claim; the V's 414km claim is the shortest in the range

No connected services on Australian cars as of CarExpert's January 2026 review (no app, remote preconditioning or over-the-air updates), and vehicle-to-load was still unconfirmed for the MY27 car at its June 2026 announcement
Reviewers found squeaks and some cheap cabin materials, a grainy hand-over from regen to the rear drum brakes, no spare wheel on any grade, and a four-star ANCAP rating versus five from Euro NCAP

summary: The Terramar VZe is the only plug-in grade in Cupra's new mid-size SUV range and, at $77,990 before on-roads, the most expensive way in Australia to buy the Volkswagen Group's 1.5-litre eHybrid drivetrain — the mechanically near-identical VW Tiguan and Tayron 200TSI eHybrid undercut it by $3,440 and $1,440 with more boot space, and the smaller Cupra Formentor VZe by $9,000. Reviewers agree the hardware delivers: 109km of electric range on Cupra Australia's ADR 81/02 figure (launch reviews quoted 110km WLTP) from a 19.7kWh usable battery, 50kW DC charging that almost no plug-in hybrid offers, and adaptive DCC Pro dampers that CarExpert found 'surprisingly comfy' on a Melbourne–Canberra run where it saw 92km of indicated electric range. Where they push back is value and detail — CarsGuide scored it 6.8 out of 10 largely on a price that sits $25,000 above a BYD Sealion 6 Premium, and CarExpert singled out an 'awful' brake pedal and strong torque steer from the front-drive layout.
pros: 109km of electric range (Cupra Australia's ADR 81/02 figure) from a 19.7kWh usable battery is among the longest of any plug-in SUV on sale here — Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV claims 86km, BYD Sealion 6 81km and Mazda CX-60 PHEV 76km — and CarExpert saw 92km indicated in Australian driving
50kW DC fast charging (10-80 per cent in about 26 minutes) alongside 11kW AC is rare on a plug-in hybrid: neither the Outlander PHEV nor the Sealion 6 can take DC at all

2,000kg braked towing is the highest rating on this drivetrain in the dataset — the VW Tiguan and Tayron 150TSI eHybrid manage 1,800kg and the Cupra Formentor VZe only 1,500kg — and it is paired with 200kW/400Nm and a 7.3sec 0-100km/h claim

The five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty is factory-backed and not conditional on servicing inside the Cupra network, the high-voltage battery is separately covered for 8 years/160,000km, and five-year capped-price servicing is quoted upfront at $2,590

Five-star ANCAP with 89 per cent adult occupant protection and 78 per cent safety assist, and at $77,990 it sits under the $80,809 ordinary LCT threshold while 11g/km CO2 clears Victoria's 120g/km green passenger car test, so no luxury car tax applies and stamp duty is charged at the flat green rate
cons: $77,990 buys the same 1.5-litre eHybrid drivetrain Volkswagen sells for $74,550 in the Tiguan 200TSI eHybrid and $76,550 in the larger, roomier Tayron — CarsGuide scored its value 6.8 out of 10 against a $52,990 BYD Sealion 6 Premium and a $50,990 drive-away GWM Haval H6 GT

The battery costs it a fifth of the boot — 400 litres against 508 litres in the petrol Terramar — and it deletes the underfloor storage and the spare wheel, leaving a puncture repair kit; CarsGuide also found rear legroom tight for a 168cm passenger

Cupra Australia's 1.8L/100km label figure only survives if you plug in every night: CarExpert averaged 5.3 and 5.9L/100km on a Melbourne–Canberra return with the battery flat for most of it, and ADAC's WLTP battery-empty figure for the 20-inch European car is 5.7L/100km from the 45-litre tank, so the running-cost case collapses for a buyer without home charging

CarExpert criticised an 'awful' brake pedal that needs excessive pressure and travel and triggered ABS unexpectedly in ordinary braking, plus torque steer that 'comes on strong' from the front-wheel-drive layout — the one Terramar that cannot be had with all-wheel drive

Plug-in hybrids lost the FBT exemption on 1 April 2025, Cupra Australia runs only 14 service centres nationally, and the brand has a documented history of deep run-out discounting — it cut more than $20,000 off the previous Formentor PHEV — so resale risk on the range-topping price is real

summary: The S07 was Australia's first Deepal model, a mid-size electric SUV sold in a single RWD grade and visibly benchmarked against the Tesla Model Y; it is now in run-out, with the 19-inch-wheel version sold out and remaining 2025-built 20-inch stock offered at $47,990 drive-away while stocks last, ahead of a teased update. CarExpert's 2025 review called it competently executed but derivative, marked down for a bouncy ride, a wide turning circle and overreactive driver-assist alerts, while praising its equipment list and quiet cabin. CarsGuide's later review found Deepal had used over-the-air updates to fix several of those early complaints, scoring it 7.4/10, even if it remains an unexciting drive with slower DC charging than key rivals.
pros: Strong standard equipment for the price, including a large tilting touchscreen, augmented-reality head-up display and 14-speaker Sony audio
Quiet, comfortable cabin with well-insulated highway cruising and good seat ergonomics
Deepal has shown it will fix early software and driver-assist niggles via over-the-air updates rather than leaving them unresolved

At $47,990 drive-away (run-out stock, 20-inch wheels) it undercuts the Tesla Model Y and Kia EV5 by thousands while offering a 7-year/160,000km vehicle warranty and an 8-year/240,000km battery warranty
cons: Bouncy ride quality with excessive body roll in corners, and a poor 11.5m turning circle for a rear-wheel-drive car
Driver-assistance systems (lane-keep, driver monitoring) were criticised as intrusive and overreactive at launch, and remain only partly resolved
Capped-price servicing runs dearer over the ownership period than rivals like the Kia EV5
Slower DC fast-charging than key mid-size EV SUV competitors: 92kW peak, about 35 minutes for 30-80%

Run-out model from Australia's newest EV brand with no resale history: the launch list price was $53,900 before on-roads, the car now sells for $47,990 drive-away, and an updated S07 has been teased, so resale value is genuinely unproven

summary: Denza's first Australian model is a body-on-frame plug-in 4x4 that reviewers consistently rate as more capable and far better equipped than its $74,990-$79,990 pricing suggests, with CarsGuide scoring it 7.8 and 4x4 Australia calling the Leopard better sorted than the larger B8. The recurring reservation is mass: at 2897-3007kg it rolls in corners and rides busily, its 490-600kg payload and 3000kg tow rating trail the diesel wagons it targets, and the 1.5-litre petrol engine only clutches to the front axle above about 80km/h, which leads CarExpert to describe its behaviour as closer to a range-extender than a conventional plug-in hybrid. Reviewers are also unanimous that the case rests on charging it — with a flat battery the trip computer settles near 11L/100km, not the 1.9L/100km on the label.
pros: 90km of electric range on the WLTC cycle rather than the NEDC figure most Chinese-derived plug-ins quote here — Chasing Cars measured 88km in urban running — and it is the rare PHEV with 100kW DC fast charging alongside 11kW AC, so the battery can be refilled on the road rather than only overnight

Real off-road hardware at the price: front and rear electronically locking differentials, low-range gearing, and 220-310mm of ground clearance via the Leopard's Disus-P hydraulic active suspension, in a body-on-frame 4x4 that undercuts a Land Rover Defender P300e plug-in by more than $50,000
400kW and 760Nm through a motor on each axle gives a claimed 4.8s 0-100km/h and 3000kg braked towing, with a manufacturer-quoted 850km combined WLTC range from the 83-litre tank

Five-star ANCAP under the current 2023-25 criteria (86% adult occupant, 95% child occupant), rated in December 2025 and valid to December 2031 — a full-criteria result rather than a carried-over older rating

Six-year/150,000km vehicle warranty with no dealer-servicing condition attached, an eight-year/160,000km battery warranty, and capped-price servicing quoted at $3542 across the first five years on 12-month/20,000km intervals
cons: The 1.9L/100km label figure only holds while the battery lasts: Denza's own charge-sustaining number is 10.9L/100km on WLTC (9.5L/100km on the more lenient NEDC), EV Central's trip computer showed 11.7L/100km with the pack depleted and Chasing Cars saw 14.0L/100km driven hard, so a buyer without home charging is running a three-tonne petrol SUV

Payload is 600kg for the base car and just 490kg for the 3007kg Leopard, which five adults and luggage will exhaust before any towball download is added — and every Australian reviewer flags the weight in the way it drives, with CarsGuide citing a busy ride and lots of body roll and the NRMA describing off-road progress as beating the earth into submission

3000kg braked towing sits 500kg under the diesel wagons and plug-in utes this car is cross-shopped against, and under the Denza B8's own 3500kg rating — 4x4 Australia and CarExpert both call the tow rating underdone for the segment

Denza is a brand-new marque in Australia with no residual-value history, a handful of metropolitan dealers and unproven long-term reliability — Chasing Cars names residuals and durability as the open questions, and the complex hydraulic suspension on the Leopard adds a repair risk used buyers will discount for

Advertised pricing is before on-road costs but the cars are widely quoted drive-away — roughly $81,500 for the base B5 and $86,700 for the Leopard in Victoria — so the $74,990 headline is about $6,500 short of what it takes to register one

summary: Denza is BYD's premium marque and the B8 — the export rebadge of China's Fangchengbao Bao 8 — is its full-size three-row plug-in 4WD, launched here in February 2026 at $91,000 before on-roads. Australian reviewers agree it massively undercuts the Toyota LandCruiser, Lexus GX and Land Rover Defender it targets while arriving with equipment those cars charge options money for, and they split hard on whether a 3290kg 425kW family wagon is a car anyone needed: CarsGuide scores it 7.5 and calls the price ultra-sharp, carsales 79/100, EV Central 4/5, while Chasing Cars gives 6.5 for a busy, unpredictable ride and CarExpert rates it 'good' but explicitly tells buyers to take the smaller B5 instead. Every review lands on the same physical fact — at just under 3.3 tonnes kerb against a 3992kg GVM there is only 702kg of payload for a seven-seater, and no reviewer thinks the DiSus-P air suspension hides the mass on-road. Off-road the hardware is genuine (310mm clearance, 890mm wading, rear locker standard and a front locker on the 6S) but 4x4 Australia notes there is no transfer case and no mechanical low range, so it leans on electronics and diff locks where a LandCruiser leans on gearing. The powertrain is a true plug-in hybrid, not a range-extender: the 2.0-litre turbo petrol clutches to the front axle through the EHS assembly and BYD's DMO system lists engine direct drive alongside EV, series and idle-generation modes, with the rear axle electric-only. The running-cost case is the sharpest in the segment for a buyer who charges nightly and collapses for one who does not — 100km of WLTC electric range, then 11.4L/100km once the battery drops under 25 per cent, the thirstiest charge-sustaining figure of any plug-in hybrid in this dataset.
pros: Prices a LandCruiser-sized, LandCruiser-capable three-row 4WD at $91,000-$97,990 before on-roads with air suspension, cross-axle lockers, nappa leather and (on the 6S) heated, cooled and massaging captain's chairs standard — CarExpert, CarsGuide, carsales and RACV all independently call the equipment-for-money the car's strongest single argument

100km of WLTC electric range from a 36.8kWh LFP blade pack and 905km of WLTC combined range on a 91-litre tank, so a buyer with home charging can do a metropolitan week without burning petrol and still cross the country at the weekend

3500kg braked towing with the towbar, hitch and wiring fitted at the factory, plus 310mm ground clearance, 890mm wading depth and a rear differential lock standard (front locker added on the 6S) — the tow rating matches a diesel LandCruiser rather than the 2500kg most plug-in SUVs manage

Its 2.0L/100km ADR 81/02 combined label clears the 3.5L/100km luxury car tax fuel-efficient test comfortably, which at these prices is worth real money: the 7S at $91,000 lands under the $91,661 fuel-efficient threshold and attracts no LCT at all, and the 6S pays on only $6,329 of its price instead of $17,181

Six-year/150,000km vehicle warranty with an eight-year/160,000km battery warranty and three years roadside assistance, and five years of capped-price servicing at $3,420 (12 months/20,000km intervals) — CarExpert notes that undercuts a LandCruiser's $4,500
cons: The 2.0L/100km window sticker is a laboratory fiction once the battery is flat: Denza's own charge-sustaining claim is 11.36L/100km on WLTC, and independent Australian testers returned about 10L/100km (CarExpert, HEV mode), 10.5L/100km (EV Central) and 11.1L/100km on the highway with the battery under 25 per cent (Chasing Cars). A buyer who cannot charge at home is running a 3.3-tonne petrol wagon

Kerb weight is 3290kg against a 3992kg GVM, leaving roughly 702kg of payload — thin for a seven-seat tourer once passengers, fuel and gear are aboard — and every reviewer criticises the body control: Chasing Cars calls the ride busy and the suspension unpredictable, CarExpert calls the car bloated and hard to control at speed and recommends the smaller B5 instead

Only 147 litres of boot with all three rows in use, which is less than a small hatchback, so the seven-seat and six-seat layouts are effectively either-or with luggage; folding the third row releases 920 litres (7S) or 902 litres (6S)

Denza Australia's window sticker quotes the superseded NEDC cycle (115km range, 2.0L/100km, 1040km combined) while its own WLTC figures are materially worse (100km, 3.9L/100km, 905km) — a buyer comparing the B8 against a WLTP-rated European rival on the advertised numbers is comparing two different tests

Denza is brand new to Australia with a handful of dealers, no residual history and no independent reliability record; RACV specifically flags long-term durability and regional support, and a debut luxury nameplate at $91,000-plus is the classic hard-depreciating case here

summary: The Mustang Mach-E is a coupe-profiled mid-size electric SUV and Ford Australia's only battery-electric passenger car, updated for 2026 with more power, a standard heat pump and a 15.5-inch portrait touchscreen. Australian reviewers consistently like how it drives — genuinely rear-drive-flavoured, precise steering, strong straight-line pace — and rate the cabin as quiet and upmarket, but they are split on the firm suspension, with CarExpert calling the ride 'far too firm' while CarsGuide found the 2026 retune acceptable. The recurring verdict is that the Select makes the value case and the Premium does not, because Chinese and Korean rivals deliver more space and equipment for less money.
pros: Extended-range Premium claims 600km WLTP from 88kWh usable, further than a Tesla Model Y Long Range RWD or Kia EV6 GT-Line, and Chasing Cars still saw 465km on a highway loop
GT makes 434kW/955Nm for 2026 (up 76kW) and undercuts a Kia EV6 GT on both price and outputs
2026 update adds a standard heat pump across the range, which reduces the cold-weather range penalty
Cheap to service for a $65k-plus EV: 12-month/15,000km intervals at roughly $158 a year, about $790 over five years
Rear-drive chassis is genuinely playful in Untamed mode, with steering CarsGuide described as light yet precise
cons: 402-litre boot is small for the class and the tapered roofline limits what fits, versus 513L in a Kia EV5 and 526L in a Polestar 4 — and the frunk shrank to 49L for 2026 to make room for the heat pump
Not rated to tow anything in Australia (0kg braked), where European Mach-Es are rated to 1000kg and rivals like the EV6 tow 1600kg
Ride is firm to the point of bump-crashiness on suburban roads, and the GT's MagneRide dampers were judged to make it worse rather than better
Real-world efficiency is poor: Chasing Cars averaged about 19kWh/100km and 19.6kWh/100km on the highway against a 17.7kWh/100km claim, which hurts anyone relying on public charging

Electronic door releases with a B-pillar button and no conventional handle, no spare wheel, and no charging cable included; Ford also ran an Australian stop-sale in late 2025 over two door-latch and related recalls

summary: The plug-in hybrid Ranger keeps the hardware that makes the diesel version work — 3500kg braked towing, a full-size dual-cab tub and the same off-road gear — and adds a mains-power outlet that Australian reviewers rate as its single best feature. The compromise is an 11.8kWh battery: testers here recorded 27-29km of real electric range against Ford's 49km Australian claim (43km WLTP), and once it is flat the 2.3-litre petrol uses 8-9L/100km or more. Opinion splits on value: Ford's MY26.5 repricing to $59,000-$70,000 recommended drive-away, with the XLT and limited-run Stormtrak dropped for a new XL, finally undercuts the BYD Shark 6, but that rival carries two and a half times the battery.
pros: Braked towing is 3500kg on every grade, matching the BYD Shark 6 Performance and GWM Cannon PHEVs, where the cheaper Shark 6 Premium is rated to 2500kg — it is a plug-in ute that can still pull a full-size caravan.
Pro Power Onboard supplies up to 6.9kW of 240V mains from the tub and cabin, which reviewers treat as a genuine replacement for a site generator or a camp setup.

Ford's MY26.5 repricing set the range at $59,000-$70,000 recommended drive-away, about $10,000 below the Sport's and Wildtrak's 2025 prices of $75,990 and $79,990 before on-road costs, and added an XL grade below where the range previously started.
Five years/unlimited km warranty with no condition to service inside the dealer network, an 8-year/160,000km battery warranty, and capped servicing at $399 per visit on 12-month/15,000km intervals.
cons: The 11.8kWh battery is about 40% of the BYD Shark 6's 29.6kWh, and Australian testers recorded 27-29km of usable electric range against the 49km Australian claim.
AC charging only and capped at 3.5kW, with no DC fast charging, so the economics collapse for anyone who cannot plug in at home overnight.

With the battery depleted, 4X4 Australia measured 8.3L/100km on a mostly highway test and CarsGuide 9.3L/100km over a week with heavy hauling, against the 2.9L/100km label; CarExpert saw about 15L/100km on a short tow.

The battery sits between the rear chassis rails and raises the tub floor about 31mm, and reviewers mark tradie configurability as limited — a standard tray or canopy fit-out is not the easy option it is on the diesel.

Payload is 934kg on the Sport and falls further on heavier grades, and CarsGuide found it dropped to 553kg once a 3500kg trailer was hitched, so an accessorised plug-in Ranger runs out of GVM quickly when towing.

summary: The Taikon 5 is the first model from Forthing, a Dongfeng sub-brand distributed in Australia by Ateco, and it landed in June 2026 as the cheapest mid-size electric SUV on sale here. The battery-electric grades share one 150kW front-drive powertrain and a 64.4kWh LFP pack rated at 427km WLTP, so the Luxury-to-Exclusive step buys trim rather than range; a range-extender version of the same body is sold alongside them and is excluded here. No Australian outlet had road-tested it at the research date, and the New Zealand launch reviews that exist split over whether the electric version's softer, less resolved ride is a fair trade for its sharper acceleration and low price.
pros: Cheapest mid-size electric SUV in Australia at launch: $38,990 drive-away for the BEV Luxury, roughly $6,000 under a GAC Aion V Premium and $8,000 under a Leapmotor C10 Style on a comparable drive-away basis
1500kg braked towing on both BEV grades per Forthing's own June 2026 spec sheet, matching a Leapmotor C10 where the similarly priced GAC Aion V has no published towing rating at all
541-litre boot expanding to 1480 litres, against 427/978 litres for a GAC Aion V and 300/1079 litres for a Chery E5

Unconditional seven-year/200,000km vehicle warranty with no dealer-servicing strings, plus an eight-year/200,000km battery warranty guaranteeing at least 70 per cent capacity; roadside assistance extends to five years but only if every scheduled service is done at a Forthing service centre

Base Luxury already includes a 14.6-inch screen, wireless CarPlay and Android Auto, 10-way power driver's seat with ventilation and massage, 19-inch alloys, 3.5kW V2L, AEB, adaptive cruise and blind-spot monitoring
cons: Unrated by ANCAP at launch, and the car ships without driver-attention monitoring or e-call, which rules out a five-star result under the current protocol
80kW peak DC charging is slow for the segment, giving 30-80 per cent in about 30 minutes against roughly 24 minutes for 10-80 per cent on a 180kW GAC Aion V
Only 14 Forthing dealers nationally (three in Victoria) and no capped-price servicing programme announced, so servicing costs and resale are entirely unproven
Forthing Australia publishes drive-away pricing only, and the campaign is restricted to new stock vehicles with no options while stock lasts, so there is no published list price for this car anywhere
No energy-consumption figure is published in Australia at all, and the 427km WLTP claim sits 27km above the 400km WLTP figure Forthing quotes for the identical 64.4kWh car in New Zealand

summary: GAC's first small car for Australia undercuts the BYD Dolphin Premium and MG 4 Essence while offering more battery, more power and far more rear legroom than either, and Australian reviewers consistently rate its ride comfort and cabin packaging above its price. The disagreement is over the software and the ownership case: CarExpert and EV Central found the touchscreen-only controls buggy and the driver-assist warnings intrusive, while CarsGuide and Chasing Cars were more forgiving and focused on the value. Everyone flags the same unknowns — a brand with no Australian resale history, roughly 30 dealers, no capped-price servicing and no ANCAP rating yet.
pros: 60kWh (58kWh usable) LFP pack and 430km WLTP range beat the BYD Dolphin Premium's 427km for $1000 less list price
150kW/210Nm and a 7.3-second 0-100km/h make it quicker than every rival under $40,000, including the MG 4 Essence 64
2750mm wheelbase and 905mm of rear legroom give it back-seat space a Toyota Corolla hatch cannot match, despite being 105mm shorter
Eight-year/unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional and two years longer than BYD's six or MG's seven
11kW AC charging as standard, against 7kW on the BYD Dolphin
cons: No ANCAP rating as at July 2026 — testing is deferred until the local eCall system goes live, so buyers are taking GAC's five-star target on trust
Climate and audio are buried in the 14.6-inch touchscreen with almost no physical controls, and reviewers report menu lag and outright bugs
87kW DC peak is slow for a 60kWh pack: about 40 minutes for 10-80 per cent, where an MG 4 64 manages a similar job faster
No capped-price servicing programme; GAC quotes $199-$640 a visit at dealer discretion and about $1607 over five years
Roughly 30 dealers nationally and no Australian resale track record, so residual values and parts supply are unproven

summary: The Aion V is the first electric SUV from GAC, which launched in Australia in December 2025, and it undercuts most mid-size rivals while quoting a longer 510km WLTP range than the Geely EX5 or BYD Atto 3. Reviewers rate the cabin quality, quietness and standard equipment highly and find the ride comfortable if unexciting, but consistently criticise the touchscreen-only controls and the intrusive driver-monitoring and speed-sign systems. Both grades share one 150kW front-drive powertrain and a 75.26kWh LFP battery, so the choice between them is purely about trim rather than range or performance.
pros: 510km WLTP range from a 75.26kWh LFP pack, ahead of the Geely EX5 (475km) and BYD Atto 3 (420km) at similar money
180kW DC charging with a claimed 24-minute 10-80 per cent, roughly double the Geely EX5's peak rate
8-year/unlimited-km vehicle warranty and 8-year/200,000km battery warranty for private buyers, longer than BYD's 6 years or Geely's 7 (commercial use drops to 5 years/150,000km)
Heat pump, V2L, panoramic sunroof, surround-view camera and heated/ventilated front seats are standard on the $42,590 base Premium
5-star ANCAP rating (2025 datestamp, valid to December 2031) applying to both grades
cons: No towing rating published in Australia at all, against 1500kg braked for a BYD Sealion 7 or Leapmotor C10
Everything runs through the 14.6-inch touchscreen, with no volume dial and mirror adjustment buried in menus
Driver-monitoring and speed-limit warnings are intrusive and reset to on at every start, a recurring complaint across Australian reviews
Highway consumption climbs past 25kWh/100km against the 16.7kWh/100km WLTP claim, so the 510km figure is urban-biased
Brand-new to Australia with about 19 dealers as at March 2026 and no capped-price servicing scheme, leaving resale and running costs unproven

summary: The EX2 is Geely's cheapest Australian model, a rear-wheel-drive electric light hatch on sale since July 2026 at $26,490 before on-road costs, and it earned a five-star ANCAP rating under the 2026 criteria. Reviewers rate the packaging highly for the money — 375 litres of boot plus a 70-litre frunk, genuine rear legroom and a cabin that reads above its price — but the dynamics divide them: CarExpert's full review and Chasing Cars both criticise the bobbing ride, body roll and grip, while RACV found its road manners solid. The objective caveats are the base car's 252km WLTP range and 14.2-second 0-100km/h.
pros: Second-cheapest new EV in Australia at $26,490 plus on-road costs, undercut only by the BYD Atto 1 Essential at $23,990
375-litre boot plus a 70-litre frunk beats the Hyundai Inster's 280 litres from a 4,135mm-long body
Five-star ANCAP rating under the 2026-28 criteria covering both grades built from June 2026 (86% crash protection), though eCall is not active until September 2027
Seven-year unlimited-kilometre vehicle warranty with eight years on the high-voltage battery, matching the Geely EX5
Efficient in practice: CarExpert measured 13.8kWh/100km on test against the Complete's 15.9kWh/100km WLTP claim
cons: The 60kW Complete takes a claimed 14.2 seconds to 100km/h, which reviewers flag as marginal for freeway merging; the 85kW Inspire is still 11.5s
252km WLTP on the Complete is the shortest range of any EV in this price band — the Inspire's 345km costs $4,500 more
DC charging peaks at just 60kW (Complete) and 80kW (Inspire), and AC at 6.6kW, so it is a poor road-trip car
CarExpert's full review found the ride bobs on smooth roads and thumps over joins, with slow steering and body roll when pushed, echoing Chasing Cars' criticism of body control and tyre grip
Not rated to tow: no braked towing capacity is published for either grade

summary: The EX5 is Geely's first model for the Australian market, a mid-size front-wheel-drive electric SUV pitched on comfort and value below better-known rivals like the Tesla Model Y. Reviewers consistently praise its quiet, cushioned ride and roomy, lounge-like rear seating, but mark it down for a smaller-than-expected boot, touchscreen-only climate controls, and driving dynamics that favour softness over sharpness. A March 2026 update (badged MY2027) brought a larger 68.39kWh battery lifting WLTP range to 475km (Complete) and 450km (Inspire), addressing the main complaint about the original 2025 launch cars.
pros: Comfortable, well-cushioned ride tuned for Australian roads
Quiet cabin with strong urban energy efficiency
Sharp pricing relative to rivals such as Leapmotor C10 and Tesla Model Y
Spacious, lounge-like rear seat comfort
Long 7-year vehicle / 8-year battery warranty
cons: Boot space (302-410L) trails key rivals like the Leapmotor C10 (581L)
Modest ~100kW DC fast-charging rate
Touchscreen-only controls for climate and headlights are fiddly
No towing rating in Australia as at November 2026, though the UK-market EX5 is rated for 750kg braked
Noticeable body roll and 'floaty' suspension feel when driven briskly

summary: The Starray EM-i is Geely's first plug-in hybrid for Australia and undercuts almost every mid-size PHEV SUV on the market, with three grades: the $37,490 Complete (83km WLTP electric range), the $41,490 Inspire Extended Range (136km) and, since September 2026, the $44,990 Inspire AWD (130km, 220kW, 1,050kg braked towing). Australian reviewers agree the powertrain and equipment list are the reasons to buy it, and that the front-drive chassis and driver-assist software are not sorted; they split on the AWD, which CarExpert found firmer and better to drive than the FWD while CarsGuide still judged its ride and handling unsuited to local roads. It is a value argument, not a driving one, resting on a brand with roughly two years of Australian sales history behind its resale values.
pros: The $41,490 Inspire Extended Range carries a 29.8kWh usable pack for 136km of WLTP electric range, within 4km of the BYD Sealion 6 Dynamic Extended Range's 140km for $5,500 less, and enough to keep most Melbourne commuters off petrol entirely
60kW DC fast charging on the Inspire Extended Range (30-80 per cent in a claimed 16 minutes) against 30kW on the Complete, so the bigger pack refills on a road trip in a coffee stop

Seven-year unlimited-kilometre warranty with no dealer-servicing condition attached, plus a separate eight-year unlimited-kilometre battery warranty guaranteed to 70 per cent capacity, and capped-price servicing quoted at $1,932 over five years

Five-star ANCAP rating (90 per cent adult occupant, 87 per cent child occupant), and all three grades, including the $44,990 Inspire AWD, sit more than $35,000 below the $80,809 ordinary LCT threshold, so no luxury car tax applies either way
Stays genuinely cheap with the battery flat: Chasing Cars recorded 5.1L/100km cumulatively over five months and 5,000km, and 95.2km of real electric range at 14.2kWh/100km on a gentle run
cons: Ride and body control are the consistent complaint: carsales calls the suspension 'far too under damped, especially from the rear' and reports porpoising, Chasing Cars describes 'pogo-like body control' on country roads, and its own long-term test concluded the ride is too soft for Australian speeds

The driver-assist software misbehaves rather than merely nags — carsales recorded the adaptive cruise cutting 30-40km/h for no reason on country roads, and multiple testers report an aggressive lane-keep that adds heavy steering weight and resets at every restart

Charge-sustaining fuel use is real money: with the battery depleted testers recorded roughly 5.9-7.0L/100km in the FWD (Chasing Cars) and the UK's Auto Express managed 6.6L/100km, so a buyer without home charging is running a 1,730-1,910kg SUV on a 1.5-litre naturally aspirated engine and the plug-in premium never pays back

The 428-litre boot is small for a mid-size SUV: NRMA singles it out as a weakness, it needs the floor removed to reach the quoted 528 litres, there is no spare wheel, only a repair kit, and the Inspire AWD's rear motor takes 72 litres of underfloor space (1,993 litres maximum against 2,065)

Geely has sold cars in Australia for about two years and has already run EOFY campaigns at 6 per cent off plus 0.88 per cent finance on the Starray EM-i and EX5, so transaction prices keep resetting and there is no resale record to anchor a residual against

summary: The GV60 is Genesis's E-GMP-based electric SUV, and the 2027 update swaps the old 77.4kWh pack for an 84kWh one while cutting the entry price by roughly $15,000 so the Advanced RWD lands under the luxury car tax threshold. Australian reviewers rate its cabin materials, noise suppression and low-speed ride among the best in the class, but consistently argue it is still priced above what an emerging luxury brand can command against the Hyundai and Kia relatives that share its hardware. The 448kW Magma adds genuine performance-car pace and heads the two-grade range, though it costs $15,000 more than a mechanically similar Ioniq 5 N.
pros: At $88,300 before on-road costs the Advanced RWD sits below the $91,661 fuel-efficient luxury car tax threshold, so no LCT is embedded in its price — a roughly $15,000 cut on the superseded Luxury grade
The 84kWh 800V pack claims 561km WLTP in the Advanced and a 10-80 per cent DC charge in 18 minutes on a 350kW charger, with 400V/800V compatibility and V2L

Ownership costs are covered: five years of complimentary scheduled servicing, roadside assistance for up to 10 years, and an 8-year/160,000km high-voltage battery warranty on top of the 5-year/unlimited-km vehicle cover
CarExpert rates the low-speed ride and suppression of wind, tyre and suspension noise as among the best of any EV, with soft-touch materials almost everywhere in the cabin
The Magma's dual-motor 448kW/740Nm drivetrain (478kW/790Nm in Boost) claims 0-100km/h in 3.4 seconds, and Genesis's spec sheet rates it to tow 2400kg braked (1600kg for the Advanced)
cons: Three of the Advanced's paint colours are a $4,000 option, which takes the car to $92,300 before on-roads and over the $91,661 luxury car tax threshold
432 litres behind the rear seats (400 in the Magma) is small for a mid-size SUV costing $88,000-plus, there is no spare wheel, and the Advanced has no internal V2L socket
The Magma asks $15,000 more than a mechanically near-identical Hyundai Ioniq 5 N, and CarExpert measured 25.6kWh/100km against the 21.5kWh/100km claim — roughly 330km of real-world range
Genesis runs only about nine Australian retail sites, all in NSW, VIC, QLD and WA, with nothing in SA, TAS, ACT or NT, which limits servicing access and thins the used-buyer pool
Body control loosens over bigger compressions on country roads, and CarExpert still judges the Advanced roughly $20,000 too expensive to be competitive against Chinese and Hyundai-group rivals

summary: Australian reviewers rate the Electrified GV70 as one of the most convincingly luxurious mid-size electric SUVs on sale, with a quiet, richly trimmed cabin, 800V charging at up to 350kW and 360kW of dual-motor pace in Boost mode. The trade-off is efficiency and packaging: 462km of WLTP range and a 503-litre boot both trail the Audi SQ6 e-tron and BMW iX3 it is cross-shopped against, and testers describe the suspension tune as comfortable and quiet but soft rather than sharp. It is sold as a single $132,718 grade at fixed national agency pricing through a retail network of roughly nine sites that reaches only New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland and Western Australia.
pros: Genesis Australia's 5-year/unlimited-kilometre warranty is genuinely unconditional — its own terms allow servicing by 'a Genesis outlet, authorised Genesis repairer or suitably qualified motor vehicle repairer' — and the high-voltage battery is separately covered for 8 years/160,000km
Five years or 75,000km of scheduled servicing is included in the purchase price, which few rivals at this price match
800V architecture charges at up to 350kW DC, taking 10-80 per cent in about 19 minutes, and adds 3.6kW vehicle-to-load outlets both inside and outside the car
Rated to tow 1,800kg braked with a 159kg towball limit, and carries a 22-litre front boot for cables on top of the 503-litre rear one
320kW/605Nm rising to 360kW/700Nm in Boost mode gives a 4.4-second 0-100km/h from the only grade offered, with no options list to navigate
cons: 462km of WLTP range and a claimed 20.0kWh/100km both trail the $129,900 Audi SQ6 e-tron (562km) and the $112,500 BMW iX3 50 xDrive (788km); CarsGuide recorded 21.0kWh/100km on test
The 503-litre boot is the smallest of its named rivals and 39 litres down on the petrol GV70's 542 litres

One grade only at $132,718 with no cheaper entry point — that is above both the $91,661 fuel-efficient luxury car tax threshold and the $75,000 FBT exemption cap, so novated-lease buyers get no EV FBT exemption

Genesis retails from around nine sites across NSW, Victoria, Queensland and WA only, leaving buyers in South Australia, Tasmania, the ACT and the Northern Territory with no local studio for sales or service
Reviewers call the suspension 'spongey in corners' — it prioritises glide over body control, where the German rivals are sharper

summary: Australian reviewers rate the Cannon Alpha PHEV as the most electric-capable dual-cab ute on sale here, pairing a 37.1kWh battery with a 3500kg braked tow rating that the BYD Shark 6 (2500kg) does not match and the Ford Ranger PHEV only equals. They are equally clear that the 2810kg kerb weight blunts it, leaving a 685kg payload and a body that shifts its mass in corners and under brakes. Verdicts split on how much that matters, from CarsGuide's 8.5 for an Ultra that impressed on a 324km loaded test to Chasing Cars' 6.5 for unpredictable throttle response and the spare wheel standing in the tub, but the running-cost case rests on home charging.
pros: 3500kg braked towing on both grades, matching a diesel dual-cab, with a 6745kg GCM

The largest plug-in battery in any Australian ute at 37.1kWh usable: GWM claims 115km electric-only on the old NEDC cycle; Chasing Cars saw 115km indicated in mixed driving, CarExpert about 85km on a highway-heavy loop
7-year/unlimited-km warranty with no servicing condition, plus 8-year battery cover and seven years of capped-price servicing and roadside assistance
50kW DC fast charging (30-80 per cent in about 24 minutes) and 6kW vehicle-to-load with GWM's V2L cable accessory
Five-star ANCAP and, at $54,990 before on-road costs for the Lux, about $1,600 under the entry Ford Ranger PHEV XL with three times its battery
cons: The 1.7L/100km label assumes a full battery every 100km: Chasing Cars recorded just over 10L/100km in hybrid mode, so a buyer without home charging is running a heavy petrol ute
685kg payload is well short of the one-tonne figure dual-cab buyers expect, and towing the full 3500kg leaves about 435kg inside the 6745kg GCM
With the battery under the floor, the steel spare sits in the tub, costing floor space and fouling tonneau covers; CarExpert, CarsGuide and Chasing Cars all call it out
At 2810kg it is about 300kg heavier than the diesel Cannon Alpha, and reviewers note mass shifting in corners, a firm ride and very conservative driver-assist systems
GWM keeps discounting it: an extra $3,000 off the drive-away price ran to 30 November 2026, a pattern that helps at purchase and hurts resale

summary: The Cannon Hi4-T is the cheapest plug-in hybrid dual-cab ute on sale here, a smaller and lighter sibling to the Cannon Alpha PHEV that keeps its 3500kg braked towing, 115km NEDC electric range and proper low-range 4x4 hardware. Early Australian reviews praise its 310kW performance, unladen ride and off-road ability, and Chasing Cars matched the electric range claim, but CarSauce recorded about 12.9L/100km on the freeway once the battery was flat. It is a two-grade range, Lux and Ultra, with the Ultra adding only comfort equipment, and it has no ANCAP rating yet.
pros: Lowest-priced plug-in ute in Australia at $48,793 before on-road costs for the Lux (backed out of GWM's Victorian drive-away price), undercutting the BYD Shark 6 and JAC Hunter PHEV
33.1kWh battery with a 115km NEDC electric-only claim that Chasing Cars matched on test and CarSauce got to about 100km, enough for most commutes without burning petrol
3500kg braked towing, 835kg payload, a dual-range transfer case and rear diff lock on both grades, with the full-size spare back under the tub
7-year/unlimited-km warranty with no servicing condition, plus 8-year battery cover, up to 110kW DC charging and three 230V outlets in the tub via vehicle-to-load
cons: The 2.4L/100km label assumes a full battery: CarSauce measured about 12.9L/100km on the freeway once depleted, so without home charging it is a thirsty 2.6-tonne petrol ute
Payload and towing cannot be used together: at 3500kg on the hitch only about 315kg of the 6400kg GCM is left for people and cargo
The battery sits under the tray and raises part of the tub floor; CarSauce notes an Australian pallet will not fit between the 1140mm wheel arches
Unrated by ANCAP, with reviewers flagging a firm ride over broken roads, average Giti tyres, weak air-conditioning and software quirks
Electric range is quoted only on the lenient NEDC cycle; there is no WLTP figure, and autotrader NZ expected 85-90km in normal use

summary: The H6 GT is the coupe-roofline sibling of the Haval H6, but its plug-in hybrid is a genuinely different car underneath: a 35.43kWh pack claiming 183km of electric range against the standard H6 PHEV's 19.09kWh and 100-106km. Reviewers agree the EV range and the 321kW/4.6sec Hi4 all-wheel-drive performance are extraordinary at the price, and agree just as consistently that the 392L boot is small for a 4.7m SUV, the brake pedal is poor and the driver-assist calibration is intrusive. The electric range is quoted on NEDC only, and independent tests returned 130-150km, so the claim is best read as an upper bound rather than a number to budget against.
pros: A 35.43kWh ternary-lithium pack claiming 183km of electric range - nearly double the 19.09kWh and 100-106km of the cheaper standard Haval H6 PHEV, and more electric range than any BYD Sealion 6 (80-125km)
321kW/642Nm from the Hi4 dual-motor all-wheel-drive system for a claimed 4.58sec 0-100km/h, quicker than the 268kW standard H6 Ultra PHEV AWD (4.8sec) and well clear of any BYD Sealion 6

DC fast charging at up to 48kW (30-80 per cent in as little as 26 minutes, GWM claim) plus 6.6kW AC, so the pack can be usefully topped up mid-trip rather than only overnight - most PHEVs in this price bracket cannot DC charge at all

Seven-year/unlimited-km warranty with no dealer-servicing condition attached, plus separate eight-year/unlimited-km cover on the drive battery and five years of roadside assistance and capped-price servicing
GWM's standard price is $54,990 drive-away (VIC private, 2026 build), and until 30 November 2026 it takes a further $2,000 off, bringing it to $52,990 drive-away
cons: The coupe roofline costs it real practicality: 392L seats-up and 1390L folded, against 560L/1445L in the standard H6 PHEV and 425L in a BYD Sealion 6, which Chasing Cars called 'piddly (for its 4727mm length)' - and rear headroom suffers too

The 0.6L/100km combined-cycle label is meaningless once the battery is flat: GWM's own charge-sustaining (Condition B) figure is 5.3-5.4L/100km, Chasing Cars measured 5.4L/100km and EV Central about 6.0L/100km, with Chasing Cars seeing 9.5L/100km at 110km/h, so a buyer who cannot charge at home is worse off than in a conventional hybrid

Electric range is quoted on the NEDC cycle only - GWM publishes no WLTP figure in Australia or New Zealand - and real-world tests returned 130-140km (EV Central), about 140km (CarsGuide) and about 150km (Chasing Cars) against the 180-183km claim

At 2045-2075kg it carries roughly 400kg more than the petrol H6 GT, there is no spare wheel on the PHEV (a repair kit only), and reviewers criticise the brake pedal - RACQ found it 'spongy, requiring a deliberate push through to the second-stage of braking'

Pricing has moved repeatedly since launch - $55,990 drive-away in 2025, $53,990, $52,990 for the April 2026 update, now $54,990 with a $2,000 bonus - which is documented evidence that resale values will be dragged down by the next campaign
