summary: The plug-in Haval H6 undercuts almost every mid-size PHEV rival, at $44,990-$50,990 drive-away for the Lux, Ultra and Ultra AWD, while claiming 100-106km of electric range and a 560L boot, and the mid-2025 update added Australian-tuned suspension. Testers agree the powertrain is smooth and genuinely quick in 268kW Hi4 all-wheel-drive form, but CarExpert and CarsGuide still mark down the ride, numb steering and an over-eager driver-assist calibration. Its case rests on being charged nightly: with a flat battery Australian testers recorded 5.8-6.2L/100km.
pros: Claims 106km of electric range (2WD, NEDC-based) from a 19.09kWh LFP pack for $44,990 drive-away in the Lux, against 80km for the similarly priced BYD Sealion 6 Essential, so most Melbourne commuters would rarely start the engine
560L boot seats-up and 1445L folded on every PHEV grade, versus 425L in the BYD Sealion 6
Seven-year/unlimited-km warranty with no dealer-servicing condition attached, plus separate eight-year/unlimited-km cover on the drive battery, against BYD's six years
DC fast charging at up to 34kW (30-80 per cent in about 28 minutes) and 3.3kW V2L are rare in a sub-$50,000 plug-in hybrid
The $50,990 drive-away Ultra PHEV AWD's Hi4 dual-motor system makes 268kW/760Nm, quicker than any Sealion 6, and every grade tows 1500kg braked
cons: The 1.0-1.1L/100km ADR label figure is meaningless once the battery is flat: Chasing Cars recorded 5.8L/100km and CarExpert 6.2L/100km with a depleted battery in the AWD, so a buyer without home charging gains little

Electric range is quoted on the NEDC-derived ADR 81/02 cycle and no WLTP figure exists (the H6 PHEV is not sold in WLTP markets); Chasing Cars measured 89km and CarExpert expects about 80km against the 100-106km claim
Reviewers repeatedly flag the driver-assist calibration, with grabby lane-keeping and random steering interventions (CarExpert, CarsGuide, Chasing Cars), plus mediocre ride and numb steering
Weight climbs from 1895kg in the Lux to about 1980kg in the Hi4 AWD, and the AWD's EV range drops to a claimed 100km
GWM sells on national drive-away pricing topped up by recurring campaigns (an extra $4,000-$5,000 off to 30 November 2026), which helps the transaction price but not resale value

summary: The Ora 5 is GWM's replacement for the axed Ora hatch: a 4.47m front-drive electric small SUV sold here in two grades, both with the same 150kW motor and 58.3kWh LFP battery. Reviewers agree it is a lot of electric car for the money and unusually quiet at highway speed, and note the rare inclusion of a space-saver spare, but they split sharply on the suspension, which CarExpert calls too firm and Chasing Cars calls floaty yet busy. The consistent criticisms are over-eager driver-monitoring alerts, a touchscreen that swallows the regen and drive-mode controls, and a claimed efficiency figure real-world testing does not reach.
pros: 435km WLTP range from a 58.3kWh usable battery for an under-$35,000 list price, against 345km for the BYD Atto 2 it is aimed at
Seven-year unlimited-kilometre warranty (eight on the battery) with capped-price servicing at $195 a visit, $1,365 across the seven years
Carries a space-saver spare wheel, still uncommon in this class, plus 6kW vehicle-to-load and 120kW DC charging for 10-80% in about 30 minutes
362-litre boot expanding to 1,060 litres with the 60/40 rear seats folded, and a 750kg braked tow rating where the MG 4 manages 500kg and the BYD Dolphin none at all

Both grades ride on the same 18-inch wheels and battery, so the $3,000 step to Ultra buys equipment (panoramic roof, powered tailgate, heated and ventilated seats, dual-zone climate) without costing range
cons: The claimed 15.5kWh/100km is optimistic: CarExpert observed about 18kWh/100km in mixed driving, which cuts real range to roughly 325km
Driver-monitoring and seatbelt warnings misfire repeatedly, and regenerative braking strength is adjustable only through the 14.6-inch touchscreen with almost no physical controls
Ride quality is the main point of reviewer disagreement - firm and bump-sensitive to CarExpert, floaty with mild rear-end instability at speed to Chasing Cars - and neither rates it as settled

Five-star ANCAP rating (November 2026) but with its weakest scores in Safe Driving (70%) and Crash Avoidance (71%): adaptive cruise failed at roundabouts and crossings, and it missed ANCAP's submerged-vehicle escape requirement

GWM publishes no list price, only a Victorian private-buyer drive-away ($33,990 Lux, $36,990 Ultra), so the list prices shown here are backed out of those figures and are estimates, not sourced numbers (CarExpert quotes $32,490 before on-roads for the Lux, which would not fit GWM's drive-away); the outgoing Ora hatch it replaces was also withdrawn after weak local sales, so expect softer resale than a BYD or MG equivalent

summary: The Tank 300 Hi4-T is the plug-in version of GWM's boxy body-on-frame off-roader, and Australian reviewers agree it is the cheapest way into a genuinely capable plug-in 4x4 — a 37.11kWh battery, a mechanical transfer case with front and rear locking diffs, and a 3000kg braked tow rating for $57,990 drive-away in Victoria, where the only other plug-in SUV rated to tow 3000kg here costs more than twice as much. They also agree on where it falls down: the drivetrain calibration is the most-criticised thing about the car, with CarsGuide calling the throttle calibration 'awful' and EV Central describing hesitation between petrol and electric power. Chasing Cars scores it 8.0/10, and every reviewer makes the same caveat, that the running-cost case rests entirely on charging at home, because once the battery is flat this is a 2.6-tonne petrol 4x4 drinking 10 to 12L/100km.
pros: A 3000kg braked tow rating with a genuine mechanical transfer case and front and rear locking differentials, from $57,990 drive-away ($54,808 before on-roads) — the only other plug-in hybrid SUV on sale in Australia rated to 3000kg is the Land Rover Defender 110 P300e, which starts at over $131,000, and every cheaper plug-in SUV tops out at 1500-2500kg

The 37.11kWh pack is the largest in any plug-in hybrid SUV under $60,000 before on-roads here, claiming 115km of electric range (NEDC), and independent testers got closer to the claim than usual: Chasing Cars saw 85-95km in stop-start driving and EV Central about 90km, enough to cover a typical commute on the plug alone

300kW and 750Nm for a claimed 6.3sec 0-100km/h, plus 50kW DC fast charging on CCS2 (30-80 per cent in about 24 minutes) and 6kW vehicle-to-load — DC charging is rare at this price and lets the pack be usefully topped up on a trip rather than only overnight
7-year/unlimited-km unconditional warranty with no dealer-servicing condition attached, plus separate 8-year/unlimited-km cover on the drive battery

Undercuts the Denza B5, its nearest plug-in off-road rival, which launched at $74,990 drive-away, by roughly $17,000, which is why reviewers repeatedly describe it as the cheapest serious plug-in hybrid four-wheel drive on sale in Australia
cons: The 1.9L/100km label figure is meaningless once the battery is flat: GWM's own low-charge figure is 8.3L/100km, and testers did worse again — CarsGuide recorded 11.0L/100km around town and 8.5L/100km in the country, Chasing Cars about 10L/100km in town, and EV Central over 12L/100km on the freeway. A buyer who cannot charge at home is running a 2.6-tonne petrol four-wheel drive

Electric range is quoted on the superseded NEDC cycle only and GWM publishes no WLTP figure for this car — it is not sold in the UK or continental Europe, so the Hi4-T has never been type-approved there and there is no European number to fall back on. Chasing Cars quotes an unsourced 100km 'WLTP' figure; read GWM's 115km as an optimistic upper bound against the 85-95km testers actually returned

Practicality is thin for a 4.76m off-roader: 360L behind the second row (1520L folded) is less than the coupe-rooflined Haval H6 GT PHEV manages, payload is only 610kg, and the 3000kg tow rating sits 500kg below GWM's own Cannon Alpha PHEV ute and a diesel Ford Everest or Toyota Prado

Drivability is the consistent complaint across Australian reviews: CarsGuide calls the throttle calibration 'awful', with little response at first and then a sudden surge that can spin the tyres on gravel, EV Central describes hesitation handing over between power sources, and Chasing Cars reports cabin creaks and a lumpy on-road ride. The part-time four-wheel-drive system also cannot be used on sealed roads

Pricing is campaign-driven rather than stable — GWM launched both grades at $55,990 and $59,990 drive-away and then added $2,000 on 1 June 2026, taking the Victorian drive-away figures to $57,990 and $61,990 ($54,808 and $58,647 before on-roads), and the Chinese-market Tank 300L facelift with a 59.6kWh pack and roughly double the electric range is already public, which would date this car sharply if it reaches Australia

summary: The Tank 500 Hi4-T is the plug-in version of GWM's Prado-sized ladder-frame 4WD and it sells as a single Ultra grade alongside the new 3.0-litre diesel Lux and Vanta and a Vanta hybrid that the diesel is replacing. Australian reviewers agree it is the most genuinely off-road-capable plug-in hybrid on sale here - dual-range mechanical 4WD, three locking differentials, 3000kg braked towing and 6kW vehicle-to-load - and agree just as consistently that the 37.11kWh pack costs it the third row, dropping a seven-seat nameplate to five seats and 640L of boot. Scores land mid-field (CarsGuide 7.0, EV Central 3.5) and the recurring complaint is that the real numbers do not follow the claims: 10.0-10.2L/100km once the battery is flat against a 2.1L/100km label, and a measured 36-37kWh/100km in EV mode that delivers about 100km against GWM Australia's 120km NEDC claim and the 110km WLTC figure.
pros: The only plug-in hybrid in Australia with real off-road hardware: a dual-range transfer case with centre diff lock plus front and rear electronic lockers, 800mm wading depth and 213mm clearance, where the plug-in seven-seaters it is cross-shopped against - Mazda CX-80, Kia Sorento PHEV - are on-road crossovers with no low range at all

3000kg braked towing at full GVM (GCM is 6430kg against a 3430kg GVM, so the tow rating does not cannibalise the load rating) plus 6kW vehicle-to-load off the traction battery, which runs a caravan and a campsite from the same car

A 37.11kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt pack good for 110km of electric-only range on the WLTC cycle (GWM Australia quotes 120km NEDC) and 50kW DC fast charging on CCS2 (30-80 per cent in 24 minutes) - most plug-in hybrids at any price cannot DC charge at all, and the Mazda CX-80 and Kia Sorento carry 17.8kWh and 13.8kWh packs
7-year/unlimited-km warranty with no dealer-servicing condition attached, backed by 8-year/unlimited-km cover on the drive battery, 7 years roadside assistance and 7 years of capped-price servicing
300kW/750Nm and a claimed 6.9sec 0-100km/h for roughly the money of a mid-spec Toyota Prado or Ford Everest, both of which are four-cylinder diesels well under half the power
cons: The third row is deleted to fit the battery, and GWM's own spec sheet proves it: the hybrid grades are 7 seats with 795L behind the second row and 98L behind the third, while the Ultra Plug-In Hybrid is 5 seats with 640L and a blank cell where the third-row figure should be - so the seven-seat Tank 500 badge does not buy you a seven-seater

The 2.1L/100km combined label is meaningless once the battery is flat: GWM's own low-charge figure is 8.4L/100km, CarsGuide measured 10.2L/100km and Chasing Cars about 10.0L/100km, so a buyer who cannot charge at home is running a 2.8-tonne petrol 4WD on 91 octane

GWM Australia still quotes electric range on the superseded NEDC cycle (120km); the WLTC figure is 110km, and the measured 36-37kWh/100km EV consumption returned by Chasing Cars and EV Central implies about 100km from the 37.11kWh pack - CarExpert also found real-world range around 100km

At 2820kg kerb the plug-in carries 215kg more than the hybrid and its payload falls from 790kg to 610kg, so a 3000kg caravan's typical 300kg ball weight consumes half of what is left; reviewers also single out body roll, an adaptive cruise system that brakes far too early and sign recognition that misread school-zone limits

GWM's $79,990 drive-away price (VIC private; $78,990 for ABN holders) is the launch sticker, but it has been discounted almost continuously - $77,990 early-bird at launch, a $4,000 end-of-financial-year cut in June 2026, $76,990 on the road per EV Central, and $1,000 off to 30 November 2026 - while the Tank 500's five-star ANCAP result was awarded to the 2024 hybrid, with GWM saying at the plug-in's launch that it was still working with ANCAP on whether the heavier PHEV is covered

summary: The Elexio is Hyundai's China-built mid-size electric SUV, mechanically close to the Kia EV5 but sold only as a single 160kW front-driver on a BYD-supplied 88.1kWh LFP pack (about 84kWh usable) in two grades, $58,990 and $61,990 before on-road costs. Australian reviewers consistently rate its locally tuned ride and steering above the EV5's, and the 562km/546km WLTP claims are among the longest at the price, but they are equally consistent that the 38-minute 10-80% DC charge and the button-free 27-inch screen are the weak points. Where opinion splits is value: some call it well-priced against a Tesla Model Y, others note a BYD Sealion 7 or Geely EX5 does the same job for less, which is why Hyundai has been running drive-away campaigns since launch.
pros: 562km WLTP on the base grade's 18-inch wheels and 546km on the Elite's 20s, longer than the Kia EV5 Air Long Range's 555km claim from the same 88.1kWh (gross) pack
Australian-tuned suspension: Chasing Cars and CarExpert both rate its body control and highway composure clearly above the mechanically related Kia EV5
506L boot expanding to 1,540L, 1,250kg braked towing and a 4kW three-pin V2L outlet, so it tows and camps like the EV5 rather than a Kona Electric (rated 0kg)
24-month/30,000km service intervals with capped-price servicing quoted at about $1,897 over four years, roughly $475 a year

Warranty is 5 years/unlimited km unconditionally, extending to 7 years/unlimited km only if every scheduled service is completed within the Hyundai dealer network; the high-voltage battery is covered 8 years/160,000km either way
cons: 400V architecture peaking at 150kW takes 38 minutes for 10-80%, against roughly half that in Hyundai's own 800V Ioniq 5, and AC charging is capped at 10kW
Tested consumption runs 20-20.8kWh/100km against the 18.2kWh/100km ADR/WLTP claim, and Chasing Cars measured a real-world 424km rather than the Elite's 546km
27-inch screen with no physical switchgear for climate or drive modes, and reviewers report the head-up display disappears behind polarised sunglasses
Front-wheel drive only at 160kW/310Nm and 8.9s to 100km/h, with no AWD grade to answer the Kia EV5 Earth or GT-Line
No spare wheel, tyre mobility kit only, and Hyundai was already advertising $57,990/$59,990 drive-away within months of launch, which points to soft early resale

summary: Australian reviewers consistently praise the Inster's cleverly packaged, unexpectedly roomy cabin and its agile, fun-to-drive character in city conditions, with several noting it feels bigger inside than its tiny footprint suggests. Value remains the main criticism: even after the 2027 price cut to $37,500 before on-roads, the Inster sits well above the BYD Dolphin, and the cut came with the heat pump and interior V2L outlet deleted. The 2027 range is thinner, down to Standard Range and Cross after Hyundai dropped the Extended Range grade and the Cross roof-basket option, while interior plastics are widely described as hard and budget-grade and the rear bench seats only two.
pros: Cleverly packaged, surprisingly spacious cabin for such a small footprint, helped by sliding and fully-folding rear seats
Agile, easy-to-park city manners with light, precise steering
Efficient: 14.3 kWh/100km WLTP for the Standard Range, and CarExpert's tester saw 11.2 kWh/100km in mixed driving
Cross adds a 49 kWh battery for 360 km WLTP (vs 327 km), 17-inch alloys, heated and ventilated front seats and a surround-view camera
Hyundai extends the 5-year warranty to 7 years when every scheduled service is done at a Hyundai dealer; EV battery covered for 8 years/160,000 km
cons: Priced well above key budget-EV rivals such as the BYD Dolphin even after the 2027 cut to $37,500 (Standard Range) and $43,500 (Cross) before on-roads
Rear seating limited to two occupants, so four seats in total
2027 cars lose the heat pump, interior V2L outlet and emergency charging cable, which hurts winter range and versatility
Hard, budget-feeling interior plastics and a sparse rear row with no vents or USB outlets
Standard Range's 327 km WLTP is modest for anything beyond city and inner-suburban driving

summary: Australian reviewers consistently rate the Ioniq 5 as one of the most complete mid-size electric SUVs on sale, praising its distinctive retro-futuristic styling, spacious and flexible cabin, and quick 800V DC charging. Ride comfort has improved with recent updates and is composed around town, though some testers still find body control loosens up over undulating country roads. The Ioniq 5 N adds genuine sports-car pace and track ability while retaining the practicality of the donor SUV, making it a standout among performance EVs, albeit at a steep price premium.
pros: Distinctive, spacious interior with a flat floor and sliding rear seats
Fast 800V charging architecture supports rapid top-ups on road trips
Comfortable, grown-up highway ride with low wind and tyre noise
Ioniq 5 N offers genuine performance-car dynamics in a practical SUV body
5-year unlimited-km warranty (7 years if every service is done at a Hyundai dealer), with the drive battery covered for 8 years / 160,000 km
cons: Body control can feel loose and float-y over undulating roads at speed
Real-world efficiency trails some rivals, particularly on the AWD and N variants
Boot space is only average for the class
Premium N Line ($83,700) and N ($115,000) sit above the $75,000 FBT exemption cap that applies from April 2027, and the N also attracts luxury car tax

summary: The Ioniq 6 is now a one-model range in Australia: Hyundai withdrew the standard Dynamiq and Epiq grades in the first half of 2026 after selling only 1,214 cars locally, and has not confirmed local timing for the facelifted non-N versions, leaving the 478kW Ioniq 6 N as the only variant you can order. Australian reviewers are close to unanimous that the N is the most convincing electric performance car at the price, rating its steering feel and rear-biased balance above the heavier Ioniq 5 N. They part company on liveability: Chasing Cars calls the ride quality excellent, while CarExpert found the damping harsh over sharp edges even in its softest setting, and all note the 371-litre boot and tight rear headroom make it the least practical N.
pros: 478kW/770Nm with N Grin Boost and 0-100km/h in 3.2 seconds undercuts a BMW M3 ($169,100) and Mercedes-AMG C63 ($187,900) by more than $50,000
487km WLTP range plus 800V charging at 10-80 per cent in 18 minutes makes it genuinely usable between track days, unlike most sub-$150k performance EVs
N e-Shift simulated eight-speed and N Drift Optimiser give real driver involvement; CarExpert and Chasing Cars both rate its handling above the Ioniq 5 N

Hyundai's 7-year/unlimited-km warranty explicitly covers non-competitive track use, but only if every service is done on time at a Hyundai dealer (otherwise 5 years); the battery is covered for 8 years/160,000km, and capped-price servicing runs around $1,312 over five years on 24-month/30,000km intervals
cons: 371-litre boot behind a structural brace that makes folding the rear seats of little use, and a separate bootlid rather than a liftback - well short of a 524-litre Toyota Camry, and less usable than the Ioniq 5 N
CarExpert recorded 22.0kWh/100km against the 18.7kWh/100km claim, cutting real touring range to roughly 380km on a 2166kg kerb weight
Suspension transmits sharp edges and potholes into the cabin even on the softest damper setting, and rear headroom is a problem for anyone over about 190cm
At $114,918 before on-road costs it sits well above the $91,661 fuel-efficient threshold, so it cannot be novated FBT-exempt the way an $80,900 Tesla Model 3 Performance can

Hyundai has pulled every standard Ioniq 6 grade from sale in Australia, so there is no cheaper version to step down to and resale is exposed to an orphaned nameplate that was recently discounted by up to $34,142

summary: Hyundai sells its three-row electric SUV in Australia as a single loaded Calligraphy grade, and reviewers agree it is the most convincing long-distance family EV on the market — 600km WLTP, 233kW DC charging and a third row adults can actually use. The disagreement is entirely about price and polish: at $119,668 before on-roads for the 2027 model year it is the dearest car Hyundai sells here, well above a comparably equipped Kia EV9 Earth, and testers split over whether the firm 21-inch ride and a cabin borrowed from much cheaper Hyundais justify it. Real-world efficiency reports vary widely, from about 12.7kWh/100km around town to 23.4kWh/100km on country touring, with Chasing Cars recording 20.8kWh/100km on its launch drive.
pros: 600km WLTP range from a 110.3kWh pack (about 106kWh usable) is the longest claim among the three-row EVs sold here, roughly 90km more than a Kia EV9 AWD grade
800V E-GMP charging takes 10-80 per cent in about 24 minutes at up to 233kW, and Australian testers have measured over 200kW
Rated to tow 2500kg braked with trailer pre-wiring and Trailer Stability Assist standard, matching the EV9 and beating most large EVs
Third row seats adults rather than children — a 175cm CarsGuide tester fit comfortably — with its own climate zone, reclining backrests and USB-C outlets
One grade means no upselling: Nappa leather, 14-speaker Bose, heat pump, head-up display, surround-view and Highway Driving Assist 2 are all standard
cons: At $119,668 plus on-road costs it clears both the $75,000 and $91,661 FBT caps, so there is no novated-lease exemption, and a Kia EV9 Earth covers the same brief for about $13,000 less

Hyundai's unconditional cover is five years/unlimited km — the advertised seven years lapses unless every scheduled service is done at an authorised Hyundai dealer, where Kia's seven years has no such condition; the battery is covered for 8 years/160,000km
Only one battery and one drivetrain are offered, with no cheaper rear-drive entry point; the six-seat layout ($2,000) and digital side mirrors ($3,000) are options, not lower-priced grades
338 litres behind the third row is modest for a 5.06m, 2.7-tonne vehicle, and there is no spare wheel at any price — only a tyre mobility kit

summary: Australian reviewers see the Kona Electric as a competent, easy-to-live-with small SUV with genuinely spacious packaging and a comfortable, relaxed ride around town, backed by Hyundai's dealer network. The Extended Range base grade is widely rated the pick of the range for value, while the Standard Range's 370km WLTP range and slow 100kW charging are seen as behind newer rivals, and the MY27 Standard Range also lost its heat pump and interior V2L outlet to hit its price. Permanent cuts of $8,000 in June 2026, plus a new $53,000 Elite slotted between Extended Range and Premium, have sharpened its position against cheaper Chinese EVs without changing the fundamental verdict: a sound, unexciting choice rather than a class leader.
pros: Spacious, well-packaged interior for the class, with strong rear legroom and a rare space-saver spare wheel
Comfortable, well-damped ride that soaks up potholes and speed bumps around town
Easy-to-use dual-screen infotainment with thoughtful right-hand-drive ergonomics
Extended Range grade ($50,000 before on-roads) undercuts the Premium by $10,000 with the same 64.8kWh battery, and its 17-inch wheels give the range's best 505km WLTP figure

Warranty extends from 5 to 7 years with unlimited km if every scheduled service is done at a Hyundai dealer; the drive battery is covered for 8 years/160,000km, and 64.8kWh grades are rated to tow 750kg braked
cons: Standard Range's 370km WLTP range looks light for a modern EV, and for MY27 it loses the heat pump (hurting cold-weather range), interior V2L and portable charging cable, and is not rated to tow
100kW DC fast-charging (10-80% in about 45 minutes) trails newer 800V rivals and is described by reviewers as not great for the segment
Chassis gets bouncy and less composed over large crests and dips at highway speed
The 19-inch wheels on Elite, Premium and Premium N Line cut WLTP range from 505km to 444km, and the Premium's $7,000 step over the Elite is questioned as not clearly justified

summary: The Jaecoo J5 EV is the battery-electric member of Chery's Jaecoo J5 small-SUV line, sold in Australia in a single fully-loaded EV Summit grade alongside separate petrol and hybrid J5s that share the body but not the drivetrain. Australian reviewers rate it as one of the cheapest ways into a well-equipped electric SUV, praising the 130kW DC charging, the eight-year warranty and a $1,520 eight-year servicing bill, while splitting over how it drives: Chasing Cars found the ride absorbent where others called it sharp, and most criticise the steering, brake feel and throttle calibration. Testers saw real-world consumption between about 14.7 and 17.5kWh/100km, which puts genuine range nearer 340-350km than the 399km WLTP figure for the UK-market twin on the same pack and 18-inch tyres.
pros: Cheapest end of the electric small-SUV class at Jaecoo's own recommended retail price of $35,990 before on-road costs, and a $36,990 national drive-away offer has been rolled over since launch (the current one runs to 30 November 2026), about $1,400 under the roughly $38,400 Victorian drive-away the list price implies
Novated-lease buyers get a standing 10% national fleet discount off the $35,990 recommended retail price through an approved fleet management organisation, on top of the BEV FBT exemption
130kW DC peak charging (30-80% in about 28 minutes) and 10.3kW three-phase AC, both well ahead of the 80kW-class Chery E5 it shares a 58.9kWh-usable LFP pack with

Eight-year unlimited-kilometre vehicle and high-voltage battery warranty, conditional only on servicing to the manufacturer's schedule, with eight years of capped-price servicing totalling $1,520; roadside assistance also runs to eight years but only if renewed at each scheduled service at an authorised Jaecoo dealer
Rated to tow 1,250kg braked on the manufacturer's own spec sheet, against the 750kg of most cheap Chinese electric SUVs including the Chery E5, BYD Atto 2 and GWM Ora 5
cons: Real-world consumption well above the rating: CarExpert saw 14.7kWh/100km, Chasing Cars 17.5kWh/100km and a 337km real-world range, against 399km WLTP

Front-drive chassis is unresolved: reviewers report very light steering with little self-centring, a squishy brake pedal with weak regeneration, an abrupt throttle at 60-80km/h and, on some test cars, torque steer under moderate throttle
Ride divides reviewers (absorbent to Chasing Cars, sharp over coarse bitumen to others), and the 235/55 R18 tyres carry a repair kit rather than a spare, where the closely related Chery E5 gets one
No ANCAP rating: reviewers at launch reported it untested, unlike the BYD Atto 2 and Kia EV3 it is cross-shopped against
Jaecoo is a 2025-vintage nameplate in Australia with no resale, parts or reliability record, and rolling drive-away campaigns work against used values

summary: The J7 SHS is Chery's Jaecoo sub-brand undercutting the plug-in hybrid mid-size SUV class on equipment-per-dollar, and for MY27 it is cheaper again and comes in three grades: Track and Summit front-drivers with about 90km of WLTP electric range from an 18.4kWh battery, and a new 260kW Summit AWD whose rear motor cuts the claimed electric range to 80km on the older NEDC test (an estimated 72km WLTP). Australian reviewers broadly agree the powertrain and the eight-year unlimited-kilometre warranty are the best parts of the car, but disagree on the chassis: CarExpert found it smooth and quiet on the highway, while Chasing Cars scored it 6.5/10 for numb steering, a stiff, noisy ride and calibration that needs work. The 340-litre boot, the missing braked tow rating and a young service network are the recurring practical objections.
pros: About 90km of WLTP electric-only range from the 18.4kWh LFP battery in the front-drive grades, more than the BYD Sealion 6 Premium AWD's 81km and enough to cover a typical Melbourne commute on electricity alone

Eight-year/unlimited-kilometre warranty with no shorter fallback term, plus eight-year unlimited-kilometre high-voltage battery cover against capacity falling below 70 per cent, longer than BYD's six-year and MG's seven-year cover
40kW DC fast charging (30-80 per cent in about 20 minutes) and 6.6kW AC charging (25-100 per cent in about 160 minutes) on every grade, unusual at this price
The new Summit AWD adds a 113kW/210Nm rear motor for 260kW and 490Nm combined, against 205kW for the front-drive grades, for $3000 more than the Summit 2WD
All three grades sit far below the $75,000 and $80,809 thresholds and their 1.3-1.9L/100km label figures pass the 3.5L/100km fuel-efficiency test, so no luxury car tax applies
cons: 340-litre boot (to the cargo cover) is well down on the 425 litres of a BYD Sealion 6, the direct cost of packaging the battery, and the SHS makes do with a tyre repair kit instead of a spare wheel

Jaecoo UK's WLTP figure is 47.1mpg (about 6.0L/100km) once the battery is depleted, not the 1.3L/100km label figure, and Chasing Cars estimated 8-9L/100km at motorway speed, so the running-cost case largely evaporates for a buyer who cannot charge at home
No braked towing rating at all on the Australian SHS (750kg unbraked only), although the same car is rated to 1500kg braked in the UK and a Sealion 6 Premium AWD tows 1300kg here

Reviewers criticise the steering as numb on centre and lacking self-centring, the regenerative braking as on/off in its strongest setting, and (Chasing Cars) the ride as stiff and noisy over small bumps with intrusive tyre noise above 80km/h

MY27 cut the Track's price by $4000 but also took away its heated and ventilated front seats, synthetic leather and surround-view camera, and the advertised drive-away prices are time-limited campaigns that keep resetting, so resale value is unproven

summary: The J8 SHS Summit is Jaecoo's flagship and its first car above $50,000: a single $59,990 (before on-road costs) seven-seat plug-in hybrid with a 34.5kWh battery, 315kW/580Nm from a 1.5-litre turbo and three motors, and a 70-litre tank that stretches combined range past 1,100km. Australian reviewers agree the equipment list and the electric range are extraordinary for the money — CarExpert measured 124km on a charge against a 134km WLTP figure — and equally agree the chassis is the weak point, describing a floaty, under-damped ride, heavy body roll and steering with no meaningful feel, none of it locally tuned. The third row is the other consistent objection: it is a 5+2 with no airbag coverage, no ISOFIX and roadside-only access, where the BYD Sealion 8 gives you all three.
pros: 134km of WLTP electric range from a 34.5kWh battery — roughly double the BYD Sealion 8's electric range and enough that most owners will only burn petrol on trips, with CarExpert observing 124km from a full charge in Australian conditions

70kW DC fast charging plus 6.6kW AC, where the BYD Sealion 8, Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV and Mazda CX-80 PHEV have no DC capability at all, so a mid-trip top-up takes about 25 minutes rather than an overnight plug-in

Eight-year/unlimited-kilometre vehicle warranty with no dealer-servicing exclusivity condition, matched by an eight-year unlimited-kilometre high-voltage battery warranty guaranteeing 70 per cent residual capacity, and eight years of capped-price servicing averaging about $485 a year

315kW/580Nm and a claimed 5.8-second 0-100km/h make it quicker than a Sealion 8 Premium AWD while towing 1600kg braked, and at $59,990 before on-roads it sits more than $30,000 below the fuel-efficient LCT threshold so no luxury car tax applies
2021 litres of cargo space with both rear rows folded, and a 738-litre load bay with just the third row down — genuinely van-like for a $60,000 seven-seater
cons: Only 200 litres behind the third row measured to the roof, and about 110 litres to the cargo cover, when all seven seats are in use — well down on the Sealion 8's 270 litres, so it cannot carry seven people and their luggage

The 1.2L/100km ADR combined label is meaningless as a running cost: CarExpert measured 6.6L/100km once the battery was flat and closer to 10L/100km in stop-start city driving, so a buyer without home charging is running a 2275kg SUV on a 1.5-litre engine at large-petrol-SUV consumption

Reviewers are unanimous on the chassis — CarsGuide calls the ride wallowy and floaty with excessive bounce over speed bumps, carsales criticises the body roll, vague steering and poor bump absorption, and EV Central found the steering too light for anything but town work; there is no Australian suspension tuning

The third row has no airbag coverage and no child-seat anchor points, headroom suits nobody taller than an average 10-year-old, and the single-fold middle seat is on the traffic side rather than the kerb side — the Sealion 8 offers third-row ISOFIX and dedicated rear climate controls

Jaecoo's electric range is quoted only as 169km NEDC in Australia, with no local WLTP homologation published; the 134km figure here comes from the identical UK-market Jaecoo 8 SHS-P, and the brand's Australian resale record above $50,000 is entirely unproven

summary: The Avenger is Jeep's first battery-electric model and its only small SUV in Australia, sold here in three front-wheel-drive grades sharing a 115kW motor and a 51kWh usable battery. Australian reviewers consistently rate it one of the better-driving cars Jeep has produced, and its light 1520kg kerb weight makes it genuinely efficient, but the same reviewers call the pricing hard to justify against Chinese and Korean rivals and single out a three-star crash rating, a bare rear seat and cheap cabin plastics. Opinion splits on whether the Jeep character and 200mm of ground clearance offset a spec sheet that a Kia EV3 or Skoda Elroq beats on range, space and safety for similar money.
pros: Efficient for a high-riding SUV: 51kWh usable stretches to 396km WLTP at a claimed 15.6kWh/100km, and Australian testers recorded 14.3kWh/100km in mixed driving — better than the claim.
Lightest car in its class at 1520kg, more than 200kg under a BYD Atto 3, which is why it matches rivals' range on a much smaller battery and why reviewers praise its steering and body control.
Genuinely more capable off-sealed-road than its rivals: 200mm of ground clearance, selectable terrain modes and hill descent control, none of which a Volvo EX30 or Kia EV3 offers.
Cheap and predictable to maintain: servicing is capped at $250 per visit at 12-month/12,500km intervals, with roadside assistance renewed for life while it is serviced through the Jeep network.
Slow sales have made it heavily negotiable — Jeep Australia has run the Longitude at $40,000 drive-away with premium paint included, roughly $16,000 below the equivalent of its $49,990 list price.
cons: Three-star ANCAP rating (shared with Euro NCAP, 2023): 59 per cent for vulnerable road user protection and 53 per cent for safety assist, with no child presence detection, against five stars for the Volvo EX30, Kia EV3 and Skoda Elroq.

Rear seat and boot are the weakest part of the car: 355L behind the second row versus 470L in a Skoda Elroq, no rear air vents, no centre armrest and no rear door pockets, so it suits couples rather than families.
Only 115kW and 260Nm for about nine seconds to 100km/h, and reviewers repeatedly criticise over-light steering and brakes that give dead travel and then bite too hard.

Ownership risk is real: Jeep Australia is down to three models with a shrinking dealer network, the Avenger sold just 92 cars here in 2025, the five-year warranty is capped at 100,000km, and $16,000 discounts point to poor resale.

summary: The Musso EV is the first genuinely affordable battery-electric dual-cab sold in Australia, a two-grade range from $60,000 drive-away ($57,130 before on-roads) for the 2WD to $64,000 for the AWD, against the $92,990-plus LDV eT60, and Australian reviewers agree it drives far better than any ladder-frame ute because it is a monocoque with independent rear suspension rather than a converted diesel. That same architecture is the catch: braked towing is 1800kg on the 2WD and 2300kg on the AWD (lifted from 1800kg in August 2026) where the Ranger PHEV and GWM Cannon Alpha PHEV both manage 3500kg, ground clearance is 181mm, and there is no low range, so reviewers read it as a tradie's or fleet runabout rather than a tow vehicle. Opinion splits on whether the money is well spent - CarsGuide scored the 2WD 7.4/10 and praised the SUV-like ride, while CarExpert found the AWD's interior hollower than the diesel Musso's and its 266kW/630Nm feeling less quick than the figures suggest.
pros: Cheapest electric ute in Australia by a wide margin: $60,000 drive-away ($57,130 before on-roads) for the 2WD against $92,990 before on-roads for the LDV eT60, and it is line-ball with the petrol-burning BYD Shark 6 and Ford Ranger PHEV rather than carrying an EV premium
905kg payload on the 2WD (805kg AWD) beats the BYD Shark 6's 790kg and the GWM Cannon Alpha PHEV's 685kg, and the self-levelling rear shocks keep it sitting flat when loaded
Capped-price servicing totals $1,996 over seven years/140,000km - about $285 a year, roughly half what a diesel dual-cab costs to maintain

KGM's seven-year/unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional (you may service outside the dealer network if you keep the invoices) and the high-voltage battery is covered for 10 years/unlimited kilometres; only the extra roadside assistance is conditional on servicing at a KGM dealer

Reviewers consistently rate the ride and steering above every ladder-frame rival - the monocoque body, McPherson-strut front and multi-link rear make it quiet and composed on broken Melbourne roads in a way a leaf-sprung HiLux is not
cons: Braked towing of 1800kg on the 2WD (180kg towball) and 2300kg on the AWD (230kg), against the 3500kg that the Ford Ranger PHEV, GWM Cannon Alpha PHEV and every mainstream diesel dual-cab offer - a 2.5-tonne caravan or a loaded car trailer is out of the question even in the AWD
No ANCAP or Euro NCAP rating at all, so a fleet or salary-packaging buyer with a five-star purchasing policy cannot order one despite the eight airbags and full driver-assist suite

Not a genuine off-roader: 181mm of ground clearance (34mm less than the diesel Musso), no low-range transfer case, the battery pack slung under the body, and the tub is about 200mm shorter than a Ranger's

KGM sold 4116 cars in Australia in 2025, down 23.7 per cent, and the only precedent for an electric ute here - the LDV eT60 - is trading around 40-50 per cent of its new price after two to three years, so residual risk on this body style is real and unproven

KGM advertises a flat national drive-away price only (the $57,130/$61,014 list prices come from data providers), the Black Edge styling pack is no longer a separate grade, and CarExpert's AWD tester recorded 21kWh/100km against the 26kWh/100km claim while CarsGuide saw 20kWh/100km urban in the 2WD against 23kWh/100km - useful in practice, but the official numbers cannot be taken at face value either way

summary: KGM's first electric SUV for Australia arrives as a single fully-equipped front-drive grade carrying the largest battery in its price class - 80.6kWh of BYD LFP Blade - but Australian reviewers agree that battery buys less range than it should, with a 462km WLTP claim that trails the smaller-batteried Geely EX5 and testers recording between 18.2 and 21.7kWh/100km. Where they part company is whether the fundamentals compensate: CarsGuide scored it 7.1/10 for interfaces that simply work and a genuinely roomy cabin, while CarExpert and The Driven both flagged missing equipment for the money and 339Nm regularly overwhelming the front tyres. The counterweight is running cost - $2,114 of capped-price servicing over seven years and an unconditional seven-year warranty - set against no ANCAP rating at all and just 168 Torres of any kind sold in Australia across the whole first half of 2025.
pros: Capped-price servicing totals $2,114 over seven years/140,000km (about $302 a year) with a complimentary first service inside six months or 5,000km, and KGM's seven-year/unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional - you may service outside the KGM dealer network provided you keep records proving the work met KGM's specification - while the BYD Blade pack carries a separate 10-year/unlimited-kilometre warranty guaranteeing at least 70 per cent state of health

The 80.6kWh battery is the biggest in the sub-$60,000 mid-size electric SUV class - Geely EX5 68.4kWh, MG S5 62kWh, BYD Atto 3 60.5kWh - and it supports 3.5kW vehicle-to-load, 120-130kW DC charging (10-80 per cent in about 37 minutes) and 10.5kW three-phase AC
1,500kg braked towing where the Geely EX5 is not rated to tow at all and the MG S5 and BYD Atto 3 stop at 750kg, plus a 465-litre boot that opens out to 1,526 litres with the rear seats folded

One grade, no options list to navigate and no cheaper trim that deletes equipment: 18-inch alloys, powered sunroof, twin 12.3-inch screens, synthetic leather, heated and ventilated front seats, 360-degree camera, eight airbags and full driver-assist including lane centring and junction-assist AEB are all standard

A $5,010 factory bonus off the recommended retail price was running at the research date, taking the car to $53,690 drive-away with metallic paint included - available for a limited time and while stocks last, so it is a buying-window discount rather than a permanent repositioning
cons: 462km WLTP from 80.6kWh is the weakest efficiency in the class - the Geely EX5 gets 475km from 68.4kWh - and CarExpert measured 21.7kWh/100km against the 18.7kWh/100km claim; worse, 462km is the identical figure KGM published for the superseded 73.4kWh pack while Europe rates the 80.6kWh car at 503km, so the Australian range claim may simply be a carried-over number

No ANCAP rating at all, and no KGM or SsangYong model is ANCAP-rated, so a fleet or salary-packaging buyer with a five-star purchasing policy cannot order one despite the eight airbags and full driver-assist suite

Front-wheel drive only with no AWD option offered, and CarsGuide, CarExpert and The Driven independently report the 339Nm overwhelming the front Nexen tyres off the line, with regenerative braking that feels inconsistent

KGM sold 168 Torres in the first half of 2025 against 24,034 Toyota RAV4s, and the brand's total 2025 Australian volume of 4,116 was down 23.7 per cent - thin dealer coverage, and a $5,010 factory bonus on new stock pushes used values down further; CarsGuide's own verdict is that rivals come 'from brands that might hold their value better'

No spare wheel (a repair kit only), climate control is touchscreen-only so you must leave CarPlay to change the temperature, and there is no built-in navigation, no wireless phone mirroring and no wireless charging pad - a cable is mandatory
