summary: The EX90 is Volvo's electric flagship and, alongside the six-seat Cadillac Vistiq, the only luxury-badged three-row battery SUV on sale in Australia. Australian reviewers are close to unanimous on the cabin, the quietness and the safety case -- ANCAP tested it in 2025 and it returned the highest adult occupant protection score of any vehicle rated that year -- but split over the ride, which CarExpert found terse on the passively sprung Plus while CarsGuide's October 2026 test of the new single-motor Plus called it comfortable. For MY27 Volvo replaced the $124,990 Plus Twin Motor with a rear-drive Plus Single Motor at $106,990 before on-road costs, on a smaller 92kWh pack with 479km of WLTP range, leaving a two-grade range topped by the $134,990 Ultra Twin Motor Performance; both still clear the $91,661 FBT threshold.
pros: ANCAP rated the EX90 five stars on 2025 test protocols with 92 per cent adult occupant protection -- the highest score of any vehicle ANCAP rated in 2025 -- plus 94 per cent child occupant protection, 82 per cent vulnerable road user and 84 per cent safety assist

Ownership costs are close to nil beyond tyres and electricity for five years: a 5-year/unlimited-kilometre unconditional warranty, 8 years of drive-battery cover, 5 years roadside assistance, and scheduled servicing to 5 years/150,000km included in the purchase price at $0

Both grades sit on the MY26 800-volt architecture: CarsGuide quotes 10-80 per cent in 24 minutes for the single-motor Plus, and the twin-motor Ultra's DC peak rose from 250kW to 350kW -- a Cadillac Vistiq, its only luxury three-row electric rival here, peaks at 130kW

The Ultra is rated to tow 2,200kg braked (the single-motor Plus 1,500kg) and both genuinely seat seven adults on individual sliding second-row seats, in a segment where the Audi and BMW alternatives at this money are five-seaters and a Mercedes-Benz EQS SUV starts at $197,200 before on-road costs

Volvo quotes a 0.29 drag coefficient and Australian testers single out the cabin as one of the quietest they have measured, with CarExpert rating its Pilot Assist and lane-keeping calibration ahead of the Polestar and Zeekr cars that share the same Geely software stack
cons: Neither grade comes near the electric-car FBT exemption: the cheapest EX90, the Plus Single Motor, is $106,990 before on-road costs, about $15,300 above the $91,661 fuel-efficient luxury car tax threshold, and about $4,600 of that sticker is luxury car tax

The MY27 Plus Single Motor at $106,990 replaced the $124,990 Plus Twin Motor in late 2026, an $18,000 cut to the range's opening price on top of a MY26 change from 400V to 800V that leaves every launch car on the slower architecture -- both point to weak early resale
Australia gets the EX90 as a seven-seater only, with no six-seat captain's-chair layout of the kind offered on the Kia EV9 GT and Cadillac Vistiq, and only 324 litres behind the third row

Reviewers disagree on the ride: CarExpert found the passively sprung Plus Twin Motor on 20-inch wheels 'a little busy and jittery' over pockmarked roads and CarsGuide's launch review found it 'bouncy over bigger bumps, especially over the rear axle', though CarsGuide's single-motor Plus test called the suspension well calibrated

The cheaper Plus Single Motor gives up the twin-motor car's pack and capability: 88kWh usable instead of 102kWh, 479km of WLTP range instead of the Ultra's 521km, and a 1,500kg tow rating instead of 2,200kg -- and even the Ultra's 521km is well short of the 570km the pre-update launch cars advertised

summary: The XC60 T8 is the plug-in half of Volvo's mid-size luxury SUV range, sold in Australia in Plus and Ultra Dark trim alongside the non-plug-in B5 mild hybrids, and the current 18.8kWh car is in its final months: Volvo has confirmed a long-range XC60 plug-in with roughly double the electric range for the second quarter of 2027. Reviewers agree it is among the calmest and best-finished cars in its class, with 81km of claimed WLTP electric range, but split on the money: at $92,990-$101,990 it is priced against a BMW X3 30e xDrive and a Mercedes-Benz GLC 350e while carrying an ageing cabin architecture and an expired ANCAP rating. The economics rest on charging at home, because with the battery flat it drinks like the petrol SUV it becomes.
pros: 81km of claimed WLTP electric range is ahead of a Mazda CX-60 PHEV's 62km or a Kia Sorento PHEV's 58km, and Chasing Cars measured just over 70km in real driving — enough that a typical Melbourne commute never wakes the engine.
340kW/709Nm and 4.8sec to 100km/h make the T8 quicker than any petrol XC60 and quicker than the BMW X3 30e xDrive it is priced against.
Rated to tow 2250kg braked, which is 250kg more than a Mazda CX-60 PHEV and unusually strong for a plug-in hybrid.
Five-year unconditional unlimited-kilometre warranty, with five years of roadside assistance.
Reviewers repeatedly single out ride comfort and noise isolation as the car's real advantage over the German plug-ins rather than outright pace.
cons: The 1.6L/100km label figure only holds if you plug in every night; EV Central saw over 8L/100km once the battery was depleted, so a buyer without home charging is paying luxury-PHEV money to run a 2.2-tonne petrol SUV.
AC charging only at 6.4kW and no DC fast-charging, so a full recharge takes hours on a wallbox and longer from a household socket — you cannot usefully top up on a road trip.

The battery pack costs boot space (468L against 505L in Chasing Cars' comparison with the regular XC60) and raises the centre tunnel enough that Chasing Cars called the middle rear seat close to unusable.

Both grades sit above the $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT threshold and far above the $75,000 FBT cap, and PHEVs lost the electric-car FBT exemption on 1 April 2025 — the novated-lease case that carried this car in 2024 no longer exists.

A long-range replacement with more than twice the electric range is due in the second quarter of 2027, which will date a car bought now; CarExpert also notes the ANCAP rating expired in December 2023.

summary: The T8 is the only plug-in XC90 — the B5 grades alongside it are 48-volt mild hybrids with no charge port — and it is currently the only seven-seat plug-in hybrid sold in Australia above $100,000, which is most of its case. Australian reviewers are close to unanimous on the driving: 340kW, air suspension as standard and a ride-handling balance carsales rated among the best it has sampled in an SUV. Where they diverge is on whether a decade-old platform justifies $130,990, and they agree the numbers are dated — about 69km of WLTP electric range when newer plug-ins clear 100km, AC-only charging, and 7.7L/100km once the battery is flat.
pros: The only seven-seat plug-in hybrid on sale in Australia above $100,000: the Audi Q7, BMW X5 xDrive50e and Mercedes-Benz GLE 450e are all five-seat in their PHEV form, and the cheaper seven-seat plug-ins (Kia Sorento PHEV, Mazda CX-80) sit a full class below on price and equipment

Braked towing is 2400kg, unusually high for a monocoque plug-in hybrid — the Kia Sorento PHEV manages 1010kg and the Mazda CX-80 PHEV 2500kg — so the battery does not cost you a caravan the way it does in most PHEV rivals

Height-adjustable four-mode air suspension is standard on both grades, and carsales rated the resulting ride-handling balance as one of the best it has experienced in an SUV, achieved on 22-inch wheels without any Australian-specific retune

Charge it and the petrol engine barely runs: CarsGuide recorded 3.4L/100km across a week of mixed driving with regular home charging, against 8.1L/100km for the mild-hybrid B5 XC90 that costs about $25,000 less

Volvo's five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional, the high-voltage battery carries a separate eight-year/160,000km cover, and capped-price servicing runs $2380 for three years or $3870 for five on 12-month/15,000km intervals
cons: Charging is AC-only through a 3.6kW onboard charger with no DC capability at all — roughly three hours on a two-phase 6.4kW wallbox, and overnight on a household socket — so a buyer without off-street parking cannot realistically keep the battery full and is left running a 2.4-tonne petrol SUV

Once the battery is depleted it drinks like what it is: carsales measured 7.7L/100km over a week-long loan, and Volvo's own European data quotes 7.2-8.0L/100km with the battery empty, against a 1.8L/100km label figure that assumes you start every trip charged

Electric range is the weak spot of the package — about 69km on WLTP, and both CarsGuide and carsales ran out of battery in the low 60s against the 77km NEDC figure Volvo Australia advertises — at a time when several cheaper plug-in hybrids claim more than 100km

The third row is genuinely awkward: there is no boot-side release, so raising the seats means climbing into the load bay or reaching through a rear door to work a heavy lever, and CarsGuide described the process as too much effort to want to repeat regularly
Boot space behind the raised third row is 262 litres, and there is no spare wheel of any kind — only a repair kit — because of the packaging demanded by the battery pack

summary: The ID.4 is Volkswagen's mid-size electric SUV, updated for MY27 with built-in navigation, the return of physical steering-wheel buttons and a bigger 79kWh usable pack in the rear-drive 210kW Pro, while the dual-motor 250kW GTX 4MOTION keeps a 77kWh usable pack. Australian reviewers praise the ride comfort, seats and efficiency but mark down the cost-cut cabin plastics and feedback-free steering, and the car is late in its life: Volkswagen has named the ID. Tiguan as its replacement, with no Australian timing yet. Both grades list under the $75,000 FBT cap, so the decision is whether the GTX's extra 40kW, all-wheel drive and 1,800kg tow rating justify $10,000 and 24km less WLTP range.
pros: The $60,990 Pro claims 546km WLTP from a 79kWh usable pack, about 80km more than a $58,900 Tesla Model Y RWD

MY27 fixes the launch car's biggest gaps: Innovision infotainment with built-in satellite navigation, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, and physical steering-wheel buttons are standard on both grades
Adaptive Chassis Control, IQ.LIGHT Matrix LED headlights, a panoramic glass roof and heated massaging front seats are standard on the base Pro
Both grades DC fast-charge at up to 175kW, and 24-month/30,000km service intervals keep six years of capped-price servicing to $1,785 (about $298 a year)
The $70,990 GTX adds 250kW and 4MOTION for 5.4s to 100km/h plus an 1,800kg braked tow rating, well clear of a Tesla Model Y's 1,588kg and the Pro's 1,000kg
cons: Late in its cycle: Volkswagen has confirmed the ID. Tiguan will replace the ID.4, Volkswagen sells it on campaign drive-away prices ($65,990 Pro, $75,990 GTX to 31 December 2026), and the ID.5 sibling is already in run-out, all of which weighs on resale

400V architecture caps DC charging at 175kW against the 800V Hyundai Ioniq 5 and Kia EV6, and real-world consumption runs well past the claim - 18.7kWh/100km on Chasing Cars' hilly launch route and about 20kWh/100km for CarsGuide
Reviewers criticise the hard, cost-cut cabin plastics and steering that gives little feedback even in Sport mode, and there is no frunk and only a tyre mobility kit instead of a spare
The GTX gives up 24km of WLTP range to the Pro (522km v 546km) for $10,000 more, and sits only $4,010 under the $75,000 FBT cap on list price
The five-star ANCAP rating rests on a 2021 Euro NCAP test of the pre-update car rather than an Australian-specific test

summary: The ID.5 is the coupe-liftback body of Volkswagen's ID.4, and it is now in run-out: Volkswagen Australia has confirmed it will not continue into MY27, so the rear-drive 210kW Pro and dual-motor 250kW GTX 4Motion are sold only from remaining MY25/MY26 dealer stock. Australian reviewers rate the Pro highly for real-world efficiency and ride refinement, but they are close to unanimous that the GTX's $10,000 premium buys less range than it costs and that the sloping roof and haptic controls cost the car genuine practicality. Both grades list under the $75,000 FBT exemption cap, though the GTX clears it by only $2,010 before dealer delivery or options.
pros: The Pro lists at $62,990 for 544km WLTP from a 77kWh usable pack, $3,000 more than the ID.4 Pro but $4,000 under a Skoda Enyaq Coupe 85 Sportline ($66,990) with similar range
Beats its own efficiency claim in Australian conditions: CarsGuide's long-term Pro averaged 15.8kWh/100km against the official 16.2-16.3kWh/100km
The dual-motor GTX 4Motion is rated to tow 1,800kg braked, matching the ID.4 GTX and Cupra Tavascan VZ and well clear of the 1,000kg rear-drive Pro

Run-out stock carries manufacturer incentives: Volkswagen is offering a free home charger and up to three months of complimentary charging on ID.5 stock through late 2026, alongside an 8-year/160,000km battery warranty
GTX adds 250kW dual-motor 4Motion and 5.4s to 100km/h, and CarsGuide rated the chassis 'resolved, refined' at 7.5/10
cons: The $72,990 GTX gives up 18km of range to the $62,990 Pro (526km v 544km WLTP) for 1.3s of 0-100km/h; both CarExpert and CarsGuide judge the cheaper car the better buy
Discontinued after MY26: only remaining dealer stock is available, colour and option choice narrows as it sells, and an orphaned body style may weigh on resale
The coupe roofline is a real practicality cost - CarsGuide's long-termer found loading a child awkward and tall loads won't fit, and folded volume drops to 1,561L against the ID.4's 1,575L
Haptic and touch controls for climate and volume draw consistent criticism (CarsGuide: they 'sometimes work and sometimes don't'), and there is no frunk and no vehicle-to-load at either grade
The GTX sits only $2,010 under the $75,000 FBT exemption cap on list price, so dealer delivery plus one option can push a novated lease past the threshold the Pro clears comfortably

summary: The Tayron eHybrid is the long-wheelbase Tiguan's plug-in sibling, and in Australia it is sold as two front-wheel-drive grades sharing a 19.7kWh usable battery good for 113-116km of claimed electric range, among the longest of any plug-in hybrid on sale here and enough that most Melbourne commuters would run it as an EV during the week. Reviewers agree on the appeal: a 705-litre boot, DC fast charging and genuinely usable EV range from $62,390 before on-road costs, which undercuts a Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV Exceed. They agree on the catch too: the battery sits where the third row would go, so unlike the petrol Tayron the eHybrid is a five-seater only, though EV Central rated it the calmer, roomier and possibly smarter buy than the smaller Tiguan eHybrid it is based on.
pros: 113-116km of claimed electric range from a 19.7kWh usable battery is the longest in the mainstream plug-in SUV class: a Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV ES claims 86km WLTP and a Mazda CX-60 PHEV 63km, and CarExpert covered a 50km loop at an indicated 0.0L/100km on battery alone
705 litres of boot with the pack installed beats a Hyundai Santa Fe Hybrid's 628 litres, and 1,915 litres with the rear seats folded (measured to the roof) is genuinely van-like for the class
40kW DC fast charging (10-80 per cent in about 30 minutes) plus 11kW AC is rare on a plug-in hybrid: the Outlander PHEV has no 11kW AC and most rivals have no DC capability at all

Volkswagen Australia's five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional, not tied to servicing inside the dealer network, and the high-voltage battery is separately covered for 8 years/160,000km

Both grades sit below the $80,809 ordinary LCT threshold and carry a 1.7-1.8L/100km, 37-38g/km combined label, well inside Victoria's 120g/km green passenger car test, so no luxury car tax applies and stamp duty is charged at the $8.40 per $200 green rate
cons: The battery occupies the third-row well, so neither eHybrid grade can be had with seven seats while the petrol Tayron can, which makes the plug-in the wrong car for the family the nameplate is otherwise aimed at

The 1.7-1.8L/100km label figure assumes you start every trip charged; once the battery is flat it is a 1.5-litre turbo hauling about 1,930kg and WLTP rates it at 5.9L/100km battery-empty on 19-inch wheels, so the running-cost case collapses for a buyer without home charging
Front-wheel drive only, with no 4MOTION eHybrid, and reviewers found the 1.5-litre engine sounds busy and feels underdone against the kerb weight once it is doing the work on its own
The 200TSI R-Line asks a $14,160 premium over the 150TSI Elegance for 50kW, a 200kg-higher tow rating, 20-inch wheels and trim, and it crosses the $75,000 mark that the 2027 FBT cap is set at
The plug-in hybrid FBT exemption ended on 1 April 2025, so the novated-lease advantage that made earlier PHEVs compelling no longer applies to this car at all

summary: Volkswagen's first affordable plug-in hybrid for Australia takes the third-generation Tiguan and adds a 19.7kWh usable battery for a claimed electric range of 115-117km, roughly double what the Outlander PHEV and Sealion 6 offer. Reviewers rate the drivetrain refinement, the 11kW AC and 40kW DC charging and the fact that most buyers will rarely wake the petrol engine, but are consistently critical of inconsistent brake and steering weighting and of a 490L boot that gives up 162L to the petrol Tiguan. Opinion splits on value: it undercuts European rivals but is roughly $20,000 more than a BYD Sealion 6 with similar equipment.
pros: 115-117km of claimed electric range (117km Elegance, 115km R-Line) from a 19.7kWh usable battery is the longest in the mainstream mid-size PHEV class - about double the Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV and BYD Sealion 6
40kW DC fast charging (10-80% in about 26 minutes) is rare among PHEVs, which mostly offer AC only; 11kW AC fills the pack in roughly 2.5 hours
At 1.6-1.7L/100km and 37-38g/km CO2 combined it clears the LCT fuel-efficient test and Victoria's 120g/km green-car duty threshold comfortably
The high-voltage battery carries an 8-year/160,000km warranty on top of the vehicle's 5-year unlimited-kilometre cover, which is unconditional and not tied to servicing at a Volkswagen dealer
200TSI R-Line is rated to tow 2000kg braked (1800kg on the Elegance), better than most plug-in hybrids in the segment
cons: The battery costs 162L of boot: 490L versus 652L in the petrol Tiguan, and the fuel tank shrinks from 58L to 45L, so touring range depends on plugging in

Once the battery is flat it is a 1873-1883kg SUV on a 1.5-litre engine - the WLTP battery-empty figure is 5.8L/100km and reviewers report around 5L/100km, so a buyer without home charging gains little over a plain petrol Tiguan
Front-wheel drive only - there is no 4MOTION eHybrid, unlike the 150TSI and 195TSI petrol grades which are all-wheel drive
Five seats only, with no seven-seat option and no spare wheel (tyre inflation kit only); buyers needing a third row are pushed to the Tayron eHybrid

The $74,550 200TSI R-Line commands a $9,960 premium over the Elegance for 50kW and little else, sits only $450 under the $75,000 FBT cap, and is about $20,000 above a comparably equipped BYD Sealion 6; the launch drive-away deals ended on 30 June 2026

summary: The XPeng G6 is a mid-size electric SUV coupe pitched squarely at the Tesla Model Y, with reviewers praising its upmarket cabin, strong tech package and genuinely quick charging on the refreshed 800V architecture. Testers rate the ride and refinement highly and note the flagship AWD Performance undercuts a comparable Model Y on price while offering vastly stronger acceleration; the facelifted range is three grades, with the Black Edition now an appearance option rather than a separate grade. The main knocks are steering that feels heavy and artificial, a chassis that doesn't quite match the Performance variant's straight-line pace, and quirks like the lack of a glovebox and a fiddly steering-column gear selector.
pros: Upmarket interior fit-out and strong tech/safety suite for the price
Fast 800V DC charging (up to 451kW on Long Range and Performance, 382kW on Standard Range) with a claimed 10-80% top-up around 12 minutes
AWD Performance variant offers Tesla Model Y Performance-rivalling pace (0-100km/h in about 4.1s) at a much lower price
Spacious rear seating with good headroom for a coupe-SUV shape, and a 571L boot (1,374L folded)
7-year unlimited-km warranty for private buyers (7yr/160,000km commercial), plus 8yr/160,000km cover on the battery and drive unit
cons: Steering feels heavy and artificial, chassis doesn't fully back up the Performance model's speed
No glovebox and limited cabin storage
Counterintuitive steering-column gear selector
Newer brand with a history of distributor changes in Australia, which may concern some buyers on parts/service continuity

summary: The Zeekr 7X is a mid-size electric SUV that Australian reviewers treat as one of the most complete Tesla Model Y alternatives on price, and the 2027 update (orders from 1 November 2026) adds 25kW, 80Nm and up to 627km WLTP range with prices unchanged at $57,900 to $72,900 before on-road costs. Reviewers agree on the packaging, charging speed and equipment but split on the flagship: CarExpert finds the Performance AWD's air suspension bouncy at freeway speeds and prefers the steel-sprung Long Range RWD, as does The Beep, while Chasing Cars praised its ride and rated it 8/10. The range is now three grades, with the former Black Special Edition reduced to a Black Edition Package option on the Performance AWD; recurring complaints are unreliable powered doors, controls buried in the 16-inch touchscreen, weak air-conditioning on hot days and the unknown resale of a brand that has only sold cars here since 2024.
pros: The $63,900 Long Range RWD is the range sweet spot: 627km WLTP from its 100kWh pack, more than a Tesla Model Y Long Range AWD ($68,900) and for less money, with The Beep recording 500-550km at a sustained 110km/h and scoring it 9/10

800V architecture with DC charging up to 450kW on the RWD and 420kW on the 100kWh grades, plus 22kW AC across the range - double or triple the 7-11kW most rivals accept - and a claimed 16-minute 10-80 per cent DC charge on the Performance AWD
Rated to tow 2000kg braked on every variant, against 1588kg for a Tesla Model Y and 1250kg for a Kia EV5, with a 539L boot, 1978L seats folded and a front boot on a 2900mm wheelbase

Ownership costs are well defined for a new brand: five-year servicing totals $2,385 on 24-month/40,000km intervals per The Beep, with a five-year unlimited-km warranty, five years roadside assistance and an 8-year/160,000km battery warranty carrying a 70 per cent state-of-health guarantee

Equipment at the price includes a 36-inch head-up display, 16-inch touchscreen, tri-zone climate and heated seats on every grade, with ventilated and massaging front seats from the Long Range up; the 2027 update adds a built-in dashcam and rear privacy glass across the range
cons: The Black Edition Package (Onyx Black paint, 20-inch black wheels, black trim and Nappa leather) is now an option on the $72,900 Performance AWD with no announced price; the 2026 Black Special Edition cost $3,000 more, and a similar charge would lift a configured car past $75,000 and out of the full novated-lease FBT exemption that applies to every base grade from 1 April 2027

Air suspension on the Performance AWD is the biggest split between testers: CarExpert says it can bounce dramatically or bang down over bumps as it auto-lowers at freeway speed and recommends the steel-sprung Long Range RWD instead, and Chasing Cars found the front seats short on lateral support

Powered doors are called unreliable by both CarExpert and Chasing Cars - they open only partway on steep driveways and CarExpert raises a finger-pinch concern - and almost every function including climate control sits in the 16-inch touchscreen

Chasing Cars measured the Performance AWD at 18.1kWh/100km on the highway and 19.7kWh/100km around town against a 17.3kWh/100km claim, so plan on roughly 480-520km rather than 544km; it and The Beep flag weak, slow air-conditioning in hot weather, and CarExpert notes no spare wheel, only a repair kit

Resale is unquantified: Zeekr has only sold cars in Australia since 2024, and the sibling Zeekr X was repriced down $5,000-$10,000 in a single model year, so there is no evidence 7X list pricing will hold despite more than 2,200 deliveries by March 2026

summary: The Zeekr X is a compact premium-badged electric SUV that Australian reviewers rate highly for cabin materials, standard equipment and outright pace, with the MY26 update adding 50kW per variant and repricing the range to flat drive-away figures of $48,900 (RWD) and $57,900 (Performance AWD). Opinion is genuinely split on the chassis: CarsGuide rates it one of the more engaging small SUVs to drive, while CarExpert and EV Central find the ride firm and the body underdamped over broken Victorian back roads. The consistent criticisms are a menu-heavy touchscreen, hyperactive driver-assistance chimes, a 405-415km WLTP range that trails cheaper rivals on real-world testing, and the ownership unknowns of a brand that only arrived in Australia in 2024.
pros: MY26 repricing to $48,900 drive-away for the RWD lands it under the Volvo EX30 and well under a BMW iX1 while adding 50kW (now 250kW) and cutting the 0-100km/h claim to 5.6 seconds

Cabin is the standout at the price: quilted leather, 13-speaker Yamaha audio and heated front and rear seats are standard, with massaging front seats and a temperature-controlled fridge on the AWD, and reviewers consistently rate the materials above mainstream rivals such as the Geely EX5 and BYD Atto 3
The RWD's 61kWh LFP pack accepts up to 230kW DC charging for a 10-80 per cent top-up in about 18 minutes, comfortably quicker than the Volvo EX30 or Kia EV3 at similar money, plus 11kW AC
365kW Performance AWD claims 0-100km/h in 3.7 seconds, quicker than anything else in the small electric SUV class
Five-star ANCAP rating, a 1600kg braked tow rating and a 404L boot that is 42L larger than the MY25 car
cons: 405-415km WLTP range is short for the money, and Australian testers recorded 16.5-20.7kWh/100km against the 15.5kWh/100km claim (carsales measured 20.7), so plan on roughly 300-350km between charges rather than 400

Driver-assistance calibration is the near-universal complaint across CarExpert, carsales and CarsGuide: overspeed warnings that repeatedly cut the audio, an attention monitor that chimes on ordinary head checks, and lane-centring that tugs at the wheel

Almost every function including drive modes, seat adjustment and climate is buried in a menu-heavy touchscreen, and reviewers report the reversing camera hijacking the display and wireless CarPlay microphone dropouts

Service and support proposition is thin for a five-year commitment: about 16 Zeekr retail and service sites nationally (three in Melbourne plus Geelong, nothing in Tasmania or the NT), MY26 servicing moved to 12-month/20,000km intervals at roughly $614 a visit and $3,072 over five years, and the standard warranty is five years unlimited km now that the seven-year pre-order offer closed on 31 May 2026, where a Volvo EX30 includes five years of free servicing

Resale is an unquantified risk on a brand first sold here in 2024, and Chasing Cars notes MY26 prices dropped $5,000-$10,000 in a single model year, which immediately devalues the outgoing cars and gives no reason to expect the MY26 pricing to hold
